div.head: ottrg.
div.p: ottrg.

THE NIAGARA SACRIFICE. It was the custom of an Indian tribe to sacrifice a beautiful maiden annually to the spirit of the ralli of Niagara.) • O'er swift Niagara's echoing shores The moon has spread her silver ray; And loud the impatient torrent roars, Expectant of its coming prey; For on this very night The fairest Indian maid must glide • Down that swift stream so fierce and wide, Must yield her to the eddying tide, And quit the realms of light. Such sacrifice by old decree Each year bath been, each year shall be. And to which fairest maid is given The meed among so many fair? Who journeying to. the Red-man's heaven, Shall shun this world of toil and care? And doth she fear to die? Fear to embark in frail canoe, And bid her tribe, her friends, adieu, Then pass, like fleetincr ghost, from view For all eternity'? . Air, no; though death itself be near,

, An Indian maiden knows not fear. Behold her calm and passive mien, Her lustrous eyes, and dusky brow! Hath ever maid more dauntless been Than she who. comes to perish now? And yet—she scarce knows why— There lurks within her inmost breast A grief which may not be represt, That he, the chief who loves her best, Should thus behold her die; Should see her borne on ruthless wave • • Beyond all hope, all power, to save. And now the fatal hour is nigh; The•lndian warriors line the stream; While, all around, the cloudless sky Is flooded with the bright moonbeam. And lo !—at signal given— A damsel fair, in drifting boat, Mown the shimmering stream doth float; They note her form, her mien they note, And rend the echoing-heaven. Loud swells the applauding shout while she . Is gliding to eternity. But see! propelled with greater force, There enters on that scene of death , A second boat : they watch its course With straining eyes and quick-drawn breath; A warrior sits therein. ' With vigorous arra his,oars he plies, His bark with heaven's own light"ning vies, And shoots like, meteor through the-skies, • The maiden's boat to win. A few strong strokes—then, side by side, They journey down the furious tide. 'Tie he! 'tishe They meet again, Nor death itself' can part them more. 'Words speak they none, for words were vain Beside yon cataract's deafening roar; On—on'—SpeedS'edch canoe. The Falls are near, the stream more fleet, The currents shelve beneath their teet, Their eves for one snort moment meet, Then both are lost to view. Vet sweet, methinks, those lovers' fate, • Whom death bath failed to separate. 'Caseell's Magazine. Le

hol, even in what was called moderation, were doing themselves an injury by spending money on things that did them no good. Money rightly spent should be spent in manufactures, in buying themselves boots and shoes and clothing, and thus giving em- ployment to other labour, which would do some- thing towards putting an end to the distress which was so prevaleht in every hand. (Hear, hears) They' frequently heard of the distress in the land, but he asked them if it was 4to be wondered at When over one hundred and twenty millions of money were yearly spent in this country on intoxicating drinks. What might that money do if invested in other in- dustries? Workingmen had it very much in their own hands whether their country should be prosperous or not. They were there to ask them for their own sakes and for the sakes of their brother men and women to give up the strong dring, and to. spend their money in makihg their own homes brighter and giving their children better food and better cloth- ing, and at the same time in employing a greater amount of labour, and thus giving those poor souls who were out of work the means of obtaining sub- sistence for themselves. (Hear, hear, and am plause.) .. Mr. JOHN DLWRY next addressed the meeting. They had come there, he said, to ask those men who dabbled with beer to give it up because they could prove by facts and not by mere tales that it wOuld benefit every one to give it up. It' would benefit the man, and it would benefit the woman, and what blessings ,it would strew in the paths of the chil- dren. That waS the way they should look at this matter, and not regard it in the purely narrow- minded way of personal blessings. (Applause.), Mr. W. icOBERTS said he felt it a great-pleasure and a great honour to stand upon that platform along with the friends who had already addressed them. It Waff evidently a sign of the times when they in Warrington had a distinguished clergyman of the Church of England willing to stand- side by side with a 'Nonconformist minister in advocating the great cause of temperance. (Hear, hear.) There was one thing which always Struck him in con- nection with tha,t, question of temperance, and that was that therecalways seemed to be the largest number of publid-houses amongst the poorest part of their population It was the case in Warring- ton, and in the neighbouring towns of Liverpool and Manchester, and in most. pth9r places. Why was it? Simply because there was more drunkenness amongst the poorer portion of the population than in any other section of the community. When they considered the depressing times they had gone through during the last five years they were bound to ask the question, was it because the people were well housed and well provided. for. He thought they would agree with him that that was not the reason. He was going to make a statement, and he challenged contradiction. He believed that a very large number of the labouring class spent on an av,erage ss, 6s, and 7s a week in intoxicating liquor. The average wage of a labouring man in a town like Warrington was, perhaps, something like .£1 a week, and out of that there was 3s 6d a week for rent. Under snob cimuinstances as these, he asked, what else cuuld happen but that the children must suffer. (Hear, hear) On Jubilee day they saw hundreds of their ragged urchins walking without either shoes Or stockings, bat they were all glad to hear that one gentleman had found some sort of hat for the children,which, though it might look rather grotesque, was a very useful kind of head-gear for the day. (Hear, hear.) In conclu- sion, Mr. Roberts said that when they hid a sober country the depression of trade would soon disap- pear. They were told that it was entirely through foreign competition, but, he did not believe it. He believed it was through the extravagant habits of our people, and the sooner they looked that mat- ter fairly in the face, the better it would be for all. (Applause.) - The Rev. G. E. CurriNG next gave a brief but vigorous address. With regard to moderate drink- ing, he pointed put that it was the example of the moderate drinker that was more potent than that of the drunkard. A drunkard was a living warning against drunkenness,•bnt when good and upright men took drink their example was likely to be very fatal to the young. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The meeting then concluded.

"There is,i ojr., window, just now, and if you'll believe me, sir, I could scarcely recognise the lineaments of your countenance as you approached the entrance to this establishment." "I der say not. But I knowed thee, Tommy." "Thank you, sir. . . . Shaving, of course ?'' "Ay; I mun have a bit taken off, for it's as rough as a yard '.rush. (Recognises the butcher at the fire- side.) Hello, Johnny, is that thee? What arto do- ing theer ?" " I'm restin' a bit." "That's reet." "Take this chair, Mr. Suthers, please! (The farmer sits down, and the barber begins to shave.) Let me see, Mr. Suthers—l think you kindly purchased Ia: hair-brush from me some time time ago, did you not?" , "I did, Tommy." "Thank you! . . . I hope, sir, that the bristles have not manifested any disposition to take leave of their original fastenings yet.' "They're o' reet up to now, Tommy.. "Thank you! . . And how do you like your new man, Mr. Suthers?" " What, little Amos o' Nell's ?" , • "Yes, sir." , "oh, I could do no good With him at o'.! He's a little shiftless, senseless, undersiz't wastrel—an' he isn't aboon th' weight of a full-groon foomart- dog !" " (The barber, who is himself a little man, is nettled at this.) "I beg your pardon'„,Mr. Sutherudlynt allow me to remark that the physical proportions of the human frame are so variable, and so insignificant, that to judge of a man's worth, or of his intellectual ability, from his altitude, or from the superficial measure- ment ot his bodily person, would be an act of the grossest injustice. • Don't you think so, Mr. Suthers?" "I do, Tommy." "Thank you, sir!" "Ay. ay," continued the farmer, " thou'rt about reet, Tommy—as -far as I con understond tho. There's foos of o' sizes. . . . But, if yon lad had bin ten feet bee, and forty stun weight, he'd ha bin a bigger foo than he is—an' he'd have had so much moor lumber to carry." "Thank you, sir! (The barber whips the cloth of. The farmer wipes his chin; and pays his penny; and is going away. The barber follows him to the door.) Now, I hope that • you will not allow any little discrepancy of opinion to sever the attachment which-exists between yourself and one who has had your hirsute interests at heart so long, Mr. Suthers." "Not a bit, Tommy—not a bit!" "Thank you, Mr. Suthers! . . . Good morn- ing! Remember me to all at home, please!" " Good mornin', Tommy."

'-TEMPERANCE MEETING AT , WARRINGTON. On Mondayevening an open-air meeting was held at Bridge-foot, under the auspices of the Warring- ton Temperance Federation. The Rev. J., Yonge presided, and the other gentlemen on the extem- porised platform were the Rev. J. J. Langham, the Rev. G. E. Cutting. Mr. W. Roberts, and Mr. John Drury. At the time appointed for opening the meeting there were very few persons present, but after the speaking had begun a considerable/number gathered round, j The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said i they had met there that night to say something to them about the important cause of temperance. They had not come there to advocate the principles of religion, but they had come to talk upon a social 1 question which affected them all more or less, and which Perhaps affected some of them very much in- deed. Theywere there underthe auspices of the War- rington Temperance Federation, which was a new society that had been started in the town for the purpose of putting new life into the old cause of temperance, which to some in that little company had been a favourite cause for a long numberof years past. They were very anxious to do all they could towards making it a more successful cause in War- rington than it was at that moment, and so all sects and all parties had united together in that society. It was a pleasing thing that people who thought differently on almost every other subject—people who had different ideaa on religion, on politics, aid he dare say different ideas on everything else—met , together in a work of that kind, because they be- lieved that the cause of temperance was one which commended itself to the sympathy and to the sup- port of all right-thinking people. (Hear, hear.) When they came to remember they would recollect that the cause of temperance had made very won- derful progress in thircountry during the last quar- ter of a century. lirdid not suppose that there was any cause in the kingdom which had made such rapid strides as the temperance cause had made dur- ing the period he had specified. It did not seem so long ago since the time when if a matiwas known to be a teetotaller he was looked upon as a sort of fanatic, as a man who was a little bit wrong in his head, because he ventured to believe that intoxicat- ing drink, though it might be very nice to the taste, was bad for the stomach, bad for the head, and bad for the homes of the people. Now it was a popular thing to be a teetotaller, and in asking them to become teetotallers that night they were asking them to come over to the popular party. In talking to them that night they must understand that they were not ask- ing them to do anything they had not done them- selves. Those who would speak to them that night ' had given up the use of those drinks for a longer or 1 shorter time, and the did not find themselves a bit the worse for having given them up. (Applause.) They did not find that they were any worse in health than they were in the past when some of them used to take moderately of those drinks to which he was referring. It used to be a very popu- lar idea, and he supposed the idea was somewhat popular still, that it was necessary for people's health that they should drink a glass of beer every day—that it was a good tonic to the system, and he did not know what besides. It used to be thought that a man could not enjoy his dinner if be did not wash it down with Greenall's or Walker's beer, or some of the other beer provided for the consump- tion of the people. (Laughter.) He was, however, perfectly free to tell them that in years gone by he used to take a glass of beerwith his dinner,and he did not find himself any the worse in health now than he was when he did. (Hear, hear.) Indeed he might be disposed to say that on the whole he be- lieved his health had been sounder and better and 'freer from ailment since he gave dp drinking the glass of beer. (Rear, hears) Therefore, having tried both sides of the question, he could commend to them the course which he was himself at present following. (Rear, hear, and applause). The Rev. J. J. LANGHAM said that on that one subject they.were all united. They were one in their determination to fight against that, the great- est enemy their country had to fear, until by God's grace they won the victory. Their object in coming hd out was to help them to help themselves TheY w prided themselves on the fact that thl„r longed to _wpm a free country, and that the:.ere Unglishman, but was it not a lamentable tact that there thousands and thousands in tht`,S4 .p.,:ref-liria were in thraldom to that cursed drink? It might be .that many of them would say that they took it in moder- ation, and therefore did no harm; but he told them that in spite of that, though they knew it not, they were in thraldom if they were to be taxed by taking that which was no use to themselves, and which tended to pauperise their country. What would they say if a law were passed in Parliament de- - them of, say one fourth of their weekly wages? If such a law were passed there would at once be a revolution in this country; and rightly so, because they were a free people, and would not stand such tyranny. Yet they who used that alco-

Hole still a young man. and though his hair is not "slivered." his skull is ; thus differing from many men andlworsien, who have no silver on their brain, but a larie supply of it in their hair. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mormay.

The House met at 4 15 p.m. Lord Cheylesmorne, who lately sat for Coven* as Mr. Eaton, took his seat on his recent creation to the peerage; and Lord Strathmore took his seat as Baron Bowes of the United Kingdom. THE SHIP CANAL BILL. The Manchester Ship Canal Money Bill was read a third time.

div.head: COERCION BILL.
div.p: THE COERCION BILL.

Lord Ammonium presented the Crimes Bill, which passed the Commons on Friday, and moved that it be read a first time.—The motion was agreed to without comment: and it was agreed to take the second reading on Thursday.

MISCELLANEOUS. The Land Trapsfer Bill was read a third time and passed, Lord I)Wpilear: moving the rejection of the measure, but not pressing his motion to a division.— The Trusts (Scotland) Act, 1867, Amendment Bill, and the Quarries Bill were also read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at 5 15 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. QUESTIONS. - -

Mr. RATICRS, in answer to Mr. Bradlaugh, could give no information as to whether letters from the Viceregal Lodei had passed through the Dublin Post Office as " Official ; paid," such letters having reference solely to Lord Londonderry's business as a coalovrner.—Mr. BRADLAVGIT said that notice had been given a week ago, giving lull time for inquiry, but he would place in the hands of the right hon. gentleman a letter, dated June 29, from the Viceroy's secretary to his lordship's agent in London. _ .

Sir JAM ES Frnorssox. in reply to Mr. John Ellis, said that no to December 31st the ccount showed the cost of Sir H. Drummond Wolff's mission to be £22,537. The account since had not yet been made up, but there was reason to believe that the expenditure, including tele- grams and all other items, would not exceed £l3OO a month, making a total 4A a little over £27,000.

NEW MEMBERS. • Mr. Aird (introduced by Lord Randolph Churchill and Mr, Segar Hunt) took his seat on his election for North- Paddington and Mr. Ballantine, who was introduced by Mr. A,rnold Morley and Mr. R. Reid, took his seat for Covehtry.• The honourable member was greeted with enthusiastic cheers from the Opposition benches.

div.head: PEERS AND ELECTIONS.
div.p: PEERS AND ELECTIONS.

_ Sir W. LAWSON called attention to an alleged breach of the rights and privileges of the House in connection with the North Paddington election. He founded his case on a paragragh in the newspapers, which stated that Lord Salisbury and Lord Rothschild had sent their carriages for the conveyance of voters. The paragraph also stated that Lord R. Churchill had done the same. Sir Wilfrid moved that as regarded the two Peers named their conduct was a breach of the order. —Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL raised the poliA of order whether there was sufficient evidence in a mere newspaper paragraph which would justify the House in proceeding, seeing that as regards himself the paragraph was quite inaccurate in stating that he had furnished carriages—This point of order came to nothing, and Mr. W. H. Sigrrtr, in the course of the de- bate which followed, said he was not prepared to any that peers could not lend their carriages for such a pur- vete at elections. He would, however, move that the orders of the day be proceeded with.L—Sir /notion was negatived on a division by 198 to 187. THE IRISH LAND BILL. MOTION FOR SECOND READING.

Mr. A, J. BALFOUR, in moving the second re,ding of the Irish Land Bill, said two bills had been brought forward sea final settlemen of the Irish land question; but the great problem was more unsettled than before. They did not propose by this bill to settle the Irish land question. They fixed their attention upon cases of grievatices and injus- tice which had arisen. At present judicial rents ran only from the date at which they were fixed. (Mr. T. Healy: It was carried by Mr. Gibson.) They proposed that henceforth the fair rent should run from the date of the application. Next, the middleman was dealt with, by giving him power tAurrender where he derived from his sub-tenants less than be paid the landlord. As to the town parks, they gave greater discretion to the Land Court. The landlord was relieved from the obliga- tion to pay rates on holdings under Xtl where -he did not receive the rents. Coming to the more important clauses, he said the first clause dealt with the question of leaseholders, and, broadly speaking, they had adopted the principle of Mr. Parnell's bill by which the advantages of the Act of 1881 were given to those leaseholders who, at the expiration of their leases, would COMP under that Act. They numbered 101,000, and only 12,000 would not come under the opera- tion of the clause. They proposed to strengthen the Court of Appeal on the land question. The fourth class of provisions gave relief to purchasers under the various Purchase Acts, and some of these clauses referred exclu- sively to Lord Ashbourne's Act, so as to facilitate the supply of the deposit, without which sale under the Act of 188.5 could not take place. He trusted these clauses would not afford food for lengthened controversy. He had now to describe the purport of two clauses which were not yet in the bill. They would give substantial relief to purchasers under the Bright clauses of the Act of 1870 and purchasers under the Glebe Act of 1869. Mr. T. W. RUSSELL asked if anything was to be done for purchasers under the Act of 1881. Mr. listroun said the clauses as drawn did not deal with them, but that would have to be rectified. Mr. PARNELL inquired how many purchasers there were under the Bright clauses. Mr. BALFOUR replied that 702 purchased under the Act of 1870, and 731 under the Act of 1880. The loans in the latter case only amounted to £240,000, and in the former to £700,000. Under the more favcibrable terms of the Act of 1885 the figures were of course much larger. Lord R. Ctnnwirit.t. aOted what charge was likely to be imposed upon the Treasury. Mr. BALFOUR believed the annual amount in the case of the glebe purchases would be £4,000. He passed now to the more controversial part which dealt with evictions. Clause 4 substituted a written notice for the execution of an ejectment. It would not be denied that painful scenes had occurred. ("House burning.") . U those scenes could be materially diminished much would be done for the peace and prosperity of Ireland. It might be asked what was gained by putting off the evictions from the date on which the notice was now served until six months after. The answer was that more than half of the tenants were on eviction immediately put back as caretakers, and only about one-fourth were finally driven from the holding. Thus under the bill there would be an immense saving of suffering to everybody concerned in the process of eviction. Turning to the equity clauses, the right hon. gentleman said Sir William 'Harcourt vehemently and violently attacked the whole class of Irish landlords—(Ministerial , cheers), judging them solely from one or two exceptional cases. ("No"). The worst that could be maintained against them was that they exacted to the utmost the legal obligations the House had sanctioned, and did not deserve to be treated as robbers simply because they did that which the law allowed all the people to whom they owed money to do to them. The scheme now submitted was contained in two different proposals—one which required the tenant to go through the form of bankruptcy to obtain the benefit of the Act, said the other which did not. Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN moved—" That this House, taking into view the circumstances set forth in the report of the Royal Commission of 1886 on the Land Acts of 1881 and 1885, and thei recommendittions of that Commission, is of opinion,that no bill for amending the laws relating to land in Ireland can be satisfactory which shall not provide not only for entitling lease- holders to the benefits of the Land Act of 1881, but also for affording such means for the revision of the judicial rent under that Act as Will meet the exigencies created by the heavy fall in agricultural values since the passing of the Aet." Be said there was a common agreement in all quarters of the House in approval of the general object and purport of the bill. Criticising the provisions, he said Clause I would leare a lease- holder without a lease and render him , a present tenant without the privileges enjoyed by present tenants. Having reminded the House of the course of evictions under the existing law, he pointed out that by this bill a legal notice would be served upon the tenant, who in this tranquil and quiet way was ipso facto converted into a caretaker. No one could doubt that at present a very large number of landlords were deterred from exer- cising their rights by the fact that they had to pass through the publicity and oditim—(Opposition cheers)— and possibly the scandal and difficulty ,of forcible evic- tions. Udder this bill he believed that thousands of. tenants would find themselves converted into caretakers before they knew where they were. They would then have six months in which to redeem and at the end of that time the same scenes and scandals would be en- acted. Mr. J. W. Lowrnen did not suppose the Government were enamoured With their own measure. It would be standing ground for a time in the deep bog of thor Irish land 14s1aaion.—Sir GEORGE CAMPBELL did not think the bill was altogether a bad bill. Lord G. risattrow regretted that Mr. Campbell- Bannerman had failed to ipdicate how the evil was to be dealt with. He did not know whether he 'proposed on behalf of the front Opposition bench to substitute the recommendations of the Cowper Conimission for those of the Government. (Mr. CAmensm-BAsnrxames: No.) Then practically the right hon, gentleman had no alter- native to submit. (Laughter.) The recommendations, moreover, would be extremely difficult to work.

Mr. I. CHAMBERLAIN said that although he intended to support the second reading of this bill, yet tv, would do sowith certain reservations which he couill hardly ex- pect any member of the Government to accept at pre- sent. Any honest and fair-minded man would admit that this was an honest attempt to deal with present indgencies. He found that Lord Fitzgerald—(laughter from the Irish members),—whom he thought hon. mem- bers 'below; the gangvray would have recognised—(re- nesried latighter)—He must remind the hon. mamba for Longford (Mr. T. M. Healy) that insultin' g interrup- tions were not arguments. Ministerial cheers.) MY- T. M. linstx : I beg to rettiind—(Loud cries of " Orarne him."—Name away.
Tun St-sarma:•l shall certainly name the hon. mem- ber if he condnues to interrupt. —Plinistprial thee., tg.)

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JULY 16, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JULY 16, 1887.

. . Mr. CHAMBERLAIN thought hon. members below the gangway would have recognised in Lord Fitzgerald a man of larger experience in reference to this question than any other politician. Lord Fitzgerald declared that it was a fair and honest attempt to deal with the most pressing necessities of the tenants of Ireland. Lord Granville said there were clauses in the bill of which he cordially approved, others in which he acquiesced, and others with which he disagreed. The bill was defec- tive in some points. Three main points required further consideration, but he thought the equitable jurisdic- tion clauses gave an absolute, satisfactory, and sum. dent remedy to tenants unable to pay and threatened with evictions. The Government had amply redeemed their promise to prevent unjust eviction taking place without the intervention of a court. He never heard anyone outside the House say a good word.for the bank- ruptcy clauses. Bankruptcy was simply a means of relieving insolvency, and the bankruptcy clauses in the bill stood by themselves. The chief objection to them had been removed in the .House of Lords, for the land- lord could not now make his tenants bankrupt. He believed the landlords hated the bankruptcy clauses, which he considered most Igenerous and of far-reaching consequences. As the Irish opposed these clauses, he advised the Government to drop them. On the motion of Mr. DILLON, the debate was ad- journed till Tuesday.' • THE LAW OF ETIDENCIL - The ATTORNBINGENERAL moved the second reading of the Law of Evidence Amendment Bill, the object of which was to enable prisoners to rive evidence in all cases. After two divi- sions the debate was adjourned, Tux TRADE MARKS BILL WU considered as emended, and read a third time. _ . _ _ .

THE MARDARINE (FRAUDULENT SALE) BILL.-011 the consideration of the Margarine (Fraudulent Sale) Bill as amended, Mr. MACLURE moved to leave out "margarine" In the title and insert " butterine."—Dr. CLARICE said in the trade the general name for the compound was margarine. ("No.")—Mr. JACOB BRIGHT said but- tenne was the buttet of the poorer classes. The poor had their susceptibilities as others had, and they looked upon this change as entirely unnecessary.—Mr. C. W. GRAY strongly disapproved of the amendment.— Sir L. PLAYFAIR maintained that "margarine" was an utterly wrong name—(hear, hear)—because it was the designation of a substance intended to Make candles stiff—(laughter)—and which had no resemblance to butter. " Butterine " contained 95 per cent, of the sub- stance used in butter, and in fact it was butter from the ox instead of butter from the cow.—After a few words from Mr. Colman, Mr. S. Hill, and Mr. Kenny, Mr. Hows said the evidence given before the Select Committee clearly proved that margarine" would be a nickname, and would not correctly represent the substance sold as butterine.—The House divided—for the amendment, 99; against, 124; majority against, 25.—The bill was then read a third time and passed amid cheers. The House adjourned at 3 20 a.m. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY.

Their lordships met at 4 p.m. BILLS PASSED.—The Royal assent was given by com- mission to seventeen public and privato accounts, including the National Debt and Local Loans Act, the Trusts (Scotland) Act (1867) Amendment Act, and the Manchester Ship Canal Act. Nnw PEEns.—Lord Monckton (Lord Galway), Earl de Montalt (Lord Hawarden), the Earl of Lonciesborough, Lord St. Levan (Sir John St. Aubyn), and Lord Basing (Mr. Sclater Booth) were introduced with the customary ceremonies, and took the oath and subscribed the roll. Lord St. Levan was introduced by Lords Stalbridge and Worthington, and Lord Basing by Lord Stanley of Preston and Lord Brabourne. A REVOLUTIONARY PROPOSAL BY THE PREMIER.

_ The Marquis of SALISBURY had a grievance to complain of in the reports in some newspapers of what occured in their Lordship's House- on the previous evening. He was made to say that Sir Henry Drummond Wolff was waiting in a state of "animated expectancy." (Laugh- ter.) That would certainly have been a very disrespectful way of speaking of Her Majesty's ambassador, and he was sure he was never guilty of it. He wished to call attention to the very bad acoustic properties of that House, and if he might propose, as Conservatives some- times did, something very revolutionary, he should like to put a fourth gentleman at the clerk's table, and make him the reporter. Lord DEirmati complained that the Press persistently ignored him. (Laughter.) Earl SPBNCICE trusted that their loydships would be induced to give early attention to the recommendations of the committee on reporting. Their report contained recommendations for the improvement of the acoustic properties of the House, and also in regard to reporting their lordships' proceedings. LAND TRANSFER BILL.

On the third reading of the Land Transfer Bill, Earl BRAUCHANP proposed. in an altered form, his amendment to the fourth sub-section of the 39th clause, which provided that in case of intestacy real estate should pass in the same way as personalty. His proposal was that the clause should not apply to any real estate of a person being an infant, or incapable of disposing of property by will. The amendment was agreed to, and other amendments havingteen inserted on the motion of the LORD CHAY- CELLOR, the bill passed. STATUE OF LORI, IDDRSLIPOIL—ADSWering Lord Mount Temple, Lord AVELAND said he had consented to the placing of the statue of the Earl of Iddesleigh in the Central Hall of the House of Parliament, in the belief that, by so doing, he was acting in accordance with the wishes of a large number of the friends of the late earl. Elitut Anvemcsn.—The Merchandise Marks Act Amend- ment Hill was brought from the Commons and read a first time.—The Commons' reasons for disagreeing with one of their Lordships' amendments to-the Municipal Corporation (Ireland) (No. 2) Hill were received, and, on the motion of Lord Mc.Nsuorrrort, the amendment was not insisted upon. The House rose at 5 55 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4 p.m. QUESTIONS.

In reply to Mr. Bowen Rowlands, Mr. Marraxws said that it was true that during the trial of the prisoners charged with being concerned in the Llanwn riot,s the wife of one of the prisoners died. The justices expressed sympathy with the defendant, but, on an objection be- ing taken to such a course, declined to allow him to go home. Subsequently the defendant had a fit. Remedies were applied, and on his recovery he was allowed to sit near a window. Ultimately the justice adjourned the case from Friday to Monday in order to allow him to go home, and the defendant thanked the court for the con- sideration shr.,wn him.

In answer to Mr. John Ellis, the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said that although it might be true that Mr. Justice O'Brien, when charging the grand jury at the current Clare Assizesisaid that the criminal business con- sisted of but few cases, he also stated that there was no improvement since the previous assizes in the state of the county, which had the bad distinction of being the worst part of Ireland for social disturbances and, disorder, and that .even the amount of actual crime was greater than before.—Mr. KENNY asked whether Mr. Justice O'Brien had not been defeated over an,d over again in the con- stituency of which he spoke in this manner 7—No answer was returned to this question.

the Board at Trod., some discussion took place with refer- emu to Holyhead harbour. The vote was ultimately agreed to. On a vote of £134,662 for buildings, fishery piers, and other works in Ireland, Mr. LABOUCHERE observed that Slate and official residences in Ireland cost £13,813. He was inclined to move the reduction of the vete by that sum, but he thought the residences should be kept in repair as they would be useful when Home Rule was established. He moved to reduce the vote by £1,030. being the ex- cess of this year over last year. After some dis- cussion the vote was postponed. On a vote of £28,000 for the House of Lords officials, Mr. LABOUCHERS moved to reduce the salary of the Lord Chancellor • by £2,000, leaving him £B,OOO pounds per annum. He con- tended that fer the work he did the Lord Chancellor was overpaid.—After some remarks firdm Mr. Bradisogh the Committee divided, when there voted for the reduction 72. against 182 —Mr. LABOUCHERE moved a rOuction of £2,100. being the amount by which the salaries of the Clerk of Plirliament, Assistant Clerk, Black Rod, and Yeo- man Usher exceeded those of the corresponding officials in the House of Commons.—After considerable discussion the motion was rejected, 120, members voting for it and 184 against it.—A vote of £33,969 for the officers of the House of Commons was under discussion at 5-45, when the debate stood adjourned.—The House adjourned at five minutes te six.
110 USE OF LORDS.—TnunsDAT.
The Lord Chancellor took hi seat at a qamrter-paat four.

THE COERCION BILL.—Lord ASHBOUR'NE moved the second reading of the Crimes Bill.—Earl GrearrviLLE spoke against the bill, but said that be and his Mends did not intend to offer any opposition, which would be impotent, preferring to !pave to Her Majesty's Government the respon- sibility of the Irish policy which they thought it their duty to adopt —The Earl of CARNARTON supported the motion, but urged that an effort should be made to improve the material condition of the people of Ireland.—Several other noble Lords took part in the discussion. which resulted is the bill being read a second time. The Committee stage wan fixed for next day. The House adjourned at a quarter mot eight.
110IISS OF COMMONS.—nauasura. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock.

QUistrrioNs.—Sir inINRY HoLLAND, in answer to a ques- tion by Mr. H. Vincent, stated the decision of the Govern• ment in the case of Sir J. Pope Hennessy, and expressed the hope that the Governor of Mauritius and his subordinates would in future work In har- mony. Sir James FEnaossbx. again inierrogated ov Mr. Bryce, said Sir H. D. Wolff intended to leave Constantinople on Saturday.—Mr. Marranyv,,s told Mr. Henniker Heaton that he had no information that the strike at Bolton was caused by the importation of foreign labour.—Mr. SMITH, in reply to Mr. NPLaren, said the Government were desirous of considering whether it would be practicable to introduce legislation directed against per- sistent molestation by men or women in the pablic streets for immoral purposes. Mr. Smith was questioned by Mr. Maclure as to the appointment of a London official to the Manchester registrarship of the Prolmte Court, and stated that Sir James Hannen censidered that he had appointed the fittest man he could select. Irma Latin BILL.—The debate on the motion for the second reading of the Irish Land Bill was resumed by Lord R Churchill, who said that at this period of the session if any legislation was adopted it must be with the general agreement and consent of all the parties in the House. He agreed with Mr Dillon and Mr T W Russell in their objec- tions to the restrictions in the first clause, and as to clause 4 he feared to give it into the hands of the Irish attorneys and agents. His Lordship freely criticised other provisions of the measure. He expressed his strong disapproval of the bankruptcy clauses, making suggestions for the relief of the tenants in regard to arrears by other means; and also urged that the position of the landlords should be core. sideted, the Land Court being empowered on the applies- tion of an embarassed 'landlord to "review with large equitable jurisdiction the charges and mortgages On his estate."—Sir W. HARCOURT said he believed that if they were asked to give a second reading to the noble lord's suggested bill there would be no opposition on the Liberal side of the House. The Liberal party bad no desire to throw out this bill ; what they wished to do, in concert with the noble lord and Mr. Chamberlain, was to make it a real bill instead of a sham bill ; and if there was any dis- position on the part of the Government to meet the views which bad been expressed on both sides the Opposition would withdraw their amendment.—Mr. GOSCHFN said the Government had their own views of the bill, which they would endeavour to maintain and to induce the House to accept. The cardinal point in the bill was that it WU a temporary measure, and they did not wish to damage the prospects of a Purchase scheme.—Among other speakers were Mr. Parnell and Mr. Gladstone. Eventually the amendment was negatived without a division, and the bill read a second time.

TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN IRELAND. TRIPLE MURDER BY A LUNATIC. A sad tragedy occurred at Rathfriland, county Down on Saturday. A saddler named James Heslop, who had been for some time in a lunatic asylum, but who had been discharged as cured a couple of years ago, left his house in the morning carrying a bill-hook. He appears to have attacked with this instrument every person he met., for no less than five men and women were muti- lated by him; three of them fatally. The victims of the homicide were a neighbour, William Spiers, add -his daughter, Maggie Smell, and Mrs. Mulholland; while Lliza Higgins and Samuel Heenan were so badly hurt that they are not expected to recover. All were hor- ribly cut and hacked, the heads of Maggie Spiers and Mrs. Mulholland being almost severed from the body. The lunatic afterwards stripped himself and jumped into the lake. He was followed and captured by a sergeant and two constables. It appears the man had been discharged from Down- patrick Asylum, as his malady ivas not chronic, and up to a fortnight ago he pursued his regular avocation. Symptoms of lunacy again appearing, he was taken charge of by some friends. On Saturday morning he obtained permission to go out to re-open his shop in the Square, Rathfriland, and he appeared then perfectly sane. After leaving the house he walked over to his own house and took down the shutters. On coming out again he was seen to have a bill-hook in his hand, and walked in the direction of Ballyroney. He met Thomas Brennon and John Herron, two carters going to Rathfriland. They spoke infpassing, whereupon Heslop made a furious attack upon them with his weapon. The men whipped their horses and drove away without being seriously injured. An old man named Samuel Hemming, however, was found shortly afterwards lying on the road with shock- ing injuries from which there was no hope of recovery. The next victim was an elderly woman named Nancy Mulholland, who was found to be frightfully muti- lated. Heslop then went into a hayfield, where a young woman named Maggie Spiers, her father, and two young men were at work with scythes. A dreadful conflict ensued as the madman rushed an the haymakers. Eventually Maggie Spiers and her father were left to confront the man, the others having fled. With one stroke he cut the girl's head nearly in two, and turned upon the father, who was felled to the ground and beaten with the handle of the implement. The maniac afterwards attacked a woman named Eliza Higgina whom he fearfully injured, leaving her uncon- scious. After this he went to a lake near, and divesting himself of his clothes, plunged into the water. On emerging, he made his way in a state of nudity to the house of a woman, who had a baby in her arms. He did not attack them, but killed a goat and returned to the lake. 'A number of people assembled, and Ileslip now and again rushed at them until the police from Rathfri- land arrived, and plunging into the lake, secured the , madman after a desperate struggle. 1

In reply to Mr:-17.1-ry. Fitnerrssox said his Imperial Majesty the Sultan was unable to receive Sir H. 1). Wolff before his departure last week, and fixed Friday, the 15th inst., for his final audience. It is not intended that his departure shall be delayed loner. Mr. BRYCE : The hon. gentleman say-s "It is not in- tended." Is the House to understand that Friday next will finally and absolutely terminate the unparalleled and undignified position which her Majesty's Govern- tnent have taken up? (Hear, hear). Sir J. FErtaussox I cannot undertake twelve any such positive undertaking, but this I can undertake to say, that when the House is fully in possession of what has taken place, in a few days, the House will be of opinion that the dignity or the interests of this country have not been compromised in any way by what has taken place. Mr. Ilaycx I shall have to repeat this question as long as the present position of things lasts. Sir WIFLRID Lewsox Will the hon. gentleman state to the House what Sir H. D. Wolff is doing now? div.head: IRISH LAND BILL.
div.p: THE IRISH LAND BILL.

The debate on the motion for the second reading of the Irish Land Bill and Mr. Campbell-Bannerman's amendment was resumed by Mr. Dillon, who said that with the excep- tion of the first clause he would reject the measure with contempt, but if the amendments, of Mr. Chamberlain were adopted by the Government he should be compelled to recon- sider his position. He feared, however, that the right hon. gentleman's Speech was only a sham, and was meant merely for the country.—Mr. T. W. RUSSELL said that if the Gov- ernment failed to make a good measure of this bill, the Irish problem would have been made more difficult to solve. His constituents believed in the ;Union, and they were also quite willing to pay a fair tent, but that rent mbst accrue from the produce of the soil, and must not be a rent designed to meet the necessities of landlords who, owing to the extravagance of their ancestors Were not the masters of their' actions. He could not throw away this bill for an empty resalution, and the question for him was whether the Government were open to reasonable amend- ments. As a Unionist, he warned the Government that the Union would not be maintained by shouting about it.—Mr. Shaw-Lefevre on behalf of the Opposition, and Sir J. Gorst for the Government, took part in the debate, the latter in- viting Mr. Russell to frame his amendments, as to which he said the House would decide whether they could be adopted, and declaring further that the Government would consider favourably any amendments suggested to them by member* who were sincere in their support of the bill. The adjournment of the debate till Tbursdarwas moved by Lord R. Cauncanz. MISCELLANEOUS. ' The Prison Officers' Superannuation (Scotland) Bill end the Sheriffs' Consolidation Bill were read a second time and the Truck Bill, as amended, was considered. the debate on several clauses being adjourned. The Hotise adjourned at 2 50 a.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDussray. .

COVENTRY,-ANOTHER LIBERAL TRIUMPH,

Party colours were freely worn, and after the early hours great excitement prevailed. Both candidates received considerable help from outside the city, the Irish party especially making strenuous efforts to bring up voters,. So high did party feeling run that it was deemed ndv'zsç.J,te to draft special constables into the borough. Mr ot. the prominent places of business were barricaded. The heaviest polling took place after one o'clock in the afternoon, and in the last hour a number of voters visited the stations. Dis- turbances occurred in several parts if the city. but they were not of an organised character, and were easily quelled. The official declaration was made about eleven o'clock, as under f Ba I I ant yn n (G.L.) Eaton (C.)

THE CRAWFORD-DILKE DIVORCE CASE.—The London correspondent of the .Dublin Express says t—l hear that Mr. Donald Crawford is about to marry a lady who in addition to great personal charms, is very wealthy. :Mr. Crawford will be remembered as the petitioner in the Dilke divorce case. '

At the Kent Assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Cave, Charles Walter. an engine driver, was indicted for the wilful murder of Florence Kate Poysden, at Teynham. Medical evidence showed that the prisoner was not in a fit state to plead, and he was ordered to be confined dur- ing her Majesty's pleasure. Two brothers, named John and Henry Simkiss, the one ten and the other twelve years of age, were drowned whilst bathing in an old colliery swag at Bradley, near Wolverhampton, on Sunday afternoon. Both the lads were unable to swim, and the place where. they were drowned was in one part of it several feet dep.

A woman named Walton was found in bed with her throat cut on Saturday at Brighton. A boy returning home to breakfast found the door locked, and getting in at the window discovered bis mother dead. His step- father, who was then missing, has since been aPPre* hended. At Maidstone Assizes, on Monday, Hy. Humphrey, 62, farm labourer, was charged with the murder of his son by shooting him at Hadlow, near Tunbridge, last Mon- day. The prisoner and deceased had been quarrelling just before the occurrence, and on a verdict of "Man- slaughter," the prisoner was sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude. -

THE CASE OF Miss Cess.—lt is understood that Sir Charles Warren, the chief Commissioner of Metropolitan Police, has issued instructions to the officers of the force directing that under no circumstances are they to take upon themselves the responsibility of prosecuting any woman on a charge of solicitation without sufficient evidence to prove her guilt

div.head: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.
div.p: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.

The show of implements opened on Friday morning, and continued open on Saturday. The steam engine trials and the cream separator trials were very satisfac- tory. The working dairy attracted a good deal of attention. _ .
The weather as gloriously fine on Saturday, but the attendance of visitors was limited. _ _

In accordance with custom, divine service was held under a large marquee on the show ground on Sunday morning. There was a large attendance of herdsmen and others engaged in connection with the show. The service was conducted by the Rev. J. Lister, Vicar of St. Andrew's, and the sermon was preached by the Bishop of Newcastle. Amongst those present were Lord More- ton, Lord and Lady Arthur Cecil, the Mayor of New. castle,'Sir B. Brown and Lady Brown. As to the position in point of merit that this year's Exhibition at Newcastle will take there cannot be two opinions after an inspection of the stock-yard, which was opened to the public on Monday. A meeting of the members of the Shorthorn Society of Great Britain and Ireland was held during the afternoon., In the absence of the president, Lord Bective was voted to the chair. From the report, read by the secretary, it appeared that the society has 1,183 members. It was stated that the 33rd volume of the "Herd Book" was in course of preparation, and that it would contain the pedigrees of 4,700 bulls and cows, with their produce. The Prince of Wales and his two sons arrived in New- castle on Monday evening. The train conveying their Royal Highnesses steamed into the Central Station about six o'clock, and at once there arose a lusty cheer from the throng that crowded the platforms. The exterior of the station was prettily decorated. Their Royal High- nesses were received by the Mayor (Sir B. C. Browne), the Sheriff (Alderman W. H. Stephenson). the Town Clerk (Mr. Hill Motutn), the Under Sheriff (Mr. John Atkinson), and several members of the Town Council.. After a cordial greeting between the Princes and the civic authorities, an address was presented to his Royal Highness. His ItorAt HIGHNESS replied RS follows :—Mr. Mayor and gentlemen.---In thanking you for your cordial address of welcome let me assure you that it gives me sincere satisfaction to revisit with my two sons a city in which we met with so hearty a reception nearly three years ago. It is a matter of unfeigned congratulation •to me that my visit to Newcastle as a member of the Council of the 'Royal Agricultural Society of England will afford me the opportunity of inspecting your exhibition —a work of the highest and most varied interest, and worthy of your great and important city. lam much gratified by the terms in which you allude to the Queen'..) I can assure you, gentlemen, that her Majesty has been profoundly touched by the manifestations of love and loyalty which have everywhere greeted her on the occa- sion of the celebration of her Jubilee. This will be an eventful year in the annals of the Queen's long and glorious reign, and indeed a memorable one in the history of our Monarchy. The spontaneous and universal marks of affection and enthusiasm which have recently been displayed towards her have, I believe, been unequalled in the case of any former sovereign of this country, and it proves conclusively not only how strong is the feeling of personal attachment to her Majesty, but how deeply seated amongst us are the sentiments of loyalty and fidelity to the monarchical form of Government, and to the existing institutions of the empire. (Cheers.) The Prince and his two sons then set out amid much applause to Plessey Station and thence to Blagdon, to the residence of Sir Matthew White-Ridley, M.P., whose guests they will be till Thursday afternoon.
Temay. ANNUAL MEETING.

The weather at Newcastle-on-Tyne continued fine on,Tuesday, though the heat was oppressive. People flocked to the Showyard in very large numbers. At eleven o'clock 4.260 persons had passed the turnstiles, as cc mpared with 2,482 at Norwich last year. Shortly after noon the Prince of Wales, accompanied by Prince Albert Victor and Prince George, arrived at the show- yard from Blagdon, Sir M. White Ridley's seat. His Royal Highness was presented with an address of welcome, and briefly replied. ,Considerable crowds had assembled along the line of route, from the Central Sta- tion to Town Moor, and the Royal party was loudly cheered as they passed through the streets and along the main avenue of ' the showyard. After a brief rest in the Royal Pavilion, the Prince and members of .the Council of the Royal Agricultural Society proceeded to the large tent to attend the annual meeting of the society. Lord Egerton of Tatton presided, and amongst those present on the platform, In addition to the Royal party, were the Duke of Northumberland, Sir M. White Ridley, Mr. J. Wilson, Lord Ravensworth, Mr. Dent-Dent, Lord Tankerville, Sir M., Lopes, Lord Boyne, Mr. Chaplin, M.P., Lord A. Cecil, the Mayor of Newcastle, Lord Arm- strong, and the Bishop of Newcastle. The PRINCE of WALES, haying presented gold medals to the owners of the five premium thoroughbred stallions at the Newcastle Spring Show, moved a vote of thanks to the Corporation of Newcastle for the admirable site provided for the show.—The DUKE Of NORTHUMBERLAND seconded the resolution, which was adopted. Sir M. White-Ridley' was elected president for the next year. Their Royal Flighnesses afterwards lunched with the Council, and then inspected the most interesting exhibi- tions in the yard, returning later to Blagdon. It was announced that Prince Albert Victor had been elected a member of the society.

div.p: GENERAL

At Bilston, on Sunday, two brothers, aged respectively eight andten, were drowned while bathing in a disused slay pitt Two marines have been committed for trial at Deal for sacrilegiously breaking into St Mary's Church, at Walmer, and stealing a sum of money. _

d bill to Confer power On Lloyd's to take lands for signal stations has been presented in the Rouse of Lords by the President of the Board of Trade. • John Thomas Ross, a' coloured man, of Baltimore, murdered Emily Brown, and then sold her body to a medical college. Be has been sentenced to be hanged. .! THE. QUEEN AND THE NAVAL RETIER;.-111 order to be present at the great naval review at Spithead, on the 23rd inst., the Queen will move the Court from Windsor Castle to Osborne on the 19th inst. ODDFELLOWSHIP.—On Monday, the annual delegated assembly of the Nottingham Ancient Imperial United Order of Oddfellows commenced its sittings at Sheffield, under the presidency of Dr. Powell, Acting Grand Master, who delivered the opening address. The order nurqbers 50,000 members. •, A DESTRUCTIVE MOORLAND FIRE.—A fire has been raging on Thorne Moors, near Doncaster, for three days. a spark from a passing train having ignited some peat stacks. The fire has spread over two miles of land. The damage, estimated at £4,000, is covered by in- surance. The Queen has addressed an autograph letter to the , Home Secretary, by whom the loyal Roman Catholic Address was presented, expressing great satisfaction at receiving the address from Irish Catholics resident in London, and saying that • her Majesty has always had ; full confidence in the loyalty of her Roman Catholic subjects, both in and out of Ireland. rAN EARNEST TRIO.—A desperate fight tool place at Harborne, near Birmingham, early on Monday, between , two yqung men who had fallen out over a young lady. I One of the combatants had his skull fractured. The girl was a witness of the fight. The asseilant was arrested but managed to escape from the police. I - -

THE GREAT MOUNTAIN FIRE IN NORTE WALES.—Mon- day's report from the scene of the mountain fire on the grouse moors of Sir Watkyn Williams-Wynn, at Ituaban. North Wales, stated that the fire was raging fiercely, and a strong wind was blowing. Several miles of mountain had been devastated, and thousands of acres of moorland and pasture, together with an immense quantity of grouse, destroyed. MANSLAUGHTER CASES AT LEICESTER.—Ai Leicester Assizes, on Monday. a hawker named George Baines was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment for killing his wife by striking her on the forehead with a bucket during a quarrel. A man named Richard Flowers was. sent to prison for eight months, and his wife Martha for five months, for causing the death of a neighbotrr; Caro- line Redder, in a quarrel about their children. BUTTERINE VERSUS MARGAMIEL—A deputation waited on Baron Henry de Worms, at the conference room of the House of Commons, on Monday, in reference to the Butter Substitutes Bill, and the alteration made therein in committee by substituting the word "margarine" for "butterine." Sir William Houldsworth, Sir Lyon Play. fair, and others, having Spoken, Baron de Worms said lie would do all he could to obtain the removal of the word "margarine" from the bill, as desired by the deputation.

EXTRLORDINA.RT SCFNR IN A CHAPEL. —An extra- ordinary scene is reported to have occurred at Millstone- lane Chapel, Leicester, on Sunday night. It appears that two men and ryvomomen during the service made grave charges against the minister, and the people rose to their feet and fighting commenced. The females ran scream- ing from the building, and three policemen had to be called in to quell the disturbance. The service was not resumed. _ _

SUSPECTED MORDICU AND MUTILATION IN LONDON.— An inquest on human remains, lately discovered in the Regent's Canal. was opened on Monday afternoon by the Middlesex coroner. The police and other witnesses having proved the finding the limbs of a female in dif- ferent parts of the canal, Inspector Hare proved the finding of the lower part of the trunk. Dr. Galloway, of Barking, stated his opinion that the portions belonged to the same body. The inquiry was adjourned for a mciath. as the Home Secretary is making special inquiries in the matter.

• Several boys were playing in some unfinished build- ings in Nottingham on Saturday a f Lerman, when a wall, which was left in a tottering state, collapsed, burying two children in the ruins. Of th ,se, Arthur Mee, aged seven, was taken out dead, his head, thighs, ribs, and shoulders being terribly crushed. The other lad escaped with comparatively slight injury.

" PARNELLISIT AND CRIME."—THE CHARGE OF Lnisa AGAINST THE "TIMFH."—The Daily Noes is informed that on Friday last Mr. Ralph Male, solicitor, of Fleet-street, commenced legal proceedings against the editor, pub- lisher and proprietor of The Times in tile action brought by dr. F. H. O'Donnell against that journal on account of the articles entitled "Parnellism and Crime."

On 'Sunday, about twenty minutes past eight, p.m, a boy, named Charles Pilkington, twelve years of age. was on a raft, having a sail upon a reservoir at The Pike estate, Bolton, along with two other boys, when Puking. ton slipped off the raft and fell into the water, being drowned before any assistance could be rendered. The unfortunate lad resided at No. 88, Platt-street, Bolton. Ties CLAIM AGAINST A PROTESTANT SISTERHOOD.— Judgment was delivered on Saturday in the' Court of Appeal in the action brought by Miss Allcard against Miss Skinner (Lady Superior of the Protestant Sister- hood of St. Mary at the Cross) to recover several thou- sand pounds which she had given to the sisterhood while she was a member of the body. Lord Justice Cotton held that the plaintiff was entitled to have the stocks which she had given refunded, on the ground that she was under the influence of the defendant and her asso- ciates when she transferred them—Lord Justice Lindley disagreed, holding that the gift was voluntary, and that by not bringing her action for five years the plaintiff rifled the gift.—Lord Justice Bower also disagreed with Lord Justice Cotton, and the appeal was dismissed with costa.

• REVIEW AT ALDEaswor.--The Queen held a grand re- view at Aldershot on Satu.day, the troops present number- ing nearly 60,000 men, of the army and reserve forces. An address was presented to the Queen by the Duke of Cam- bridge on behalf of the army, waich her Majesty accepted .with pleasure, remarking that the army, whenever called upon during her reign, had never failed to justify the con- fidence and earn the gratitude of herself and peeple ; and if called upon, the auxiliary forces would ales justify that confidence, but she earnestly desired that peace mightattend the remainder of her reign. At the conclusion of the march past, which lasted three bourn, her Majesty returned to Windsor.

THX CASS CASZ INQUIRY.—The official inquiry into the conduct of Police Constable Endacott, in connection with the arrest of Mini Case. was opened at Scotland Yard on Monday. Sir Charles Warren presided, Mr. Horace Smith Recorder of Lincoln, assisting him as legal aeseseor. Mr B. St. John Wonthor represented P.C. Endacott. and Mr J. P. Grain and Mr. F. M. Abrahams Miss Caps and Madame Bowman. Endacott, Miss Caea, and Madame Bowman were not present at the opening. On the application of Mr. B. St. John Wontnor. who stated that he was only instructed that morning, the case was adjourned. The inquiry was resumed at Scotland Yard on Tueeday morning. Miss Cass stated she was 24 years of age. She Was born at Grantham and afterwards, with her parents, removed to Stockton. She entered Madame Bowman's employ on June 4th, havlng been staying at Forestgate for three weeks previously. She knew nothing of the London streets, and had never been in Regent-street alone before June 2S:h. at hen she was arres- ted. She had never spoken to gentlemen in any London street, nor had she walked about with another girl. She narrated the circumstances of her arrest, statirg that Enda. colt persisted to her that she had been in company with another girl, who had escaped him. When she denied this be said it was Vie, and at the polin, etath-n he told her several times not to tell ljes. She then detailed being hailed out by Madame Bowman and her treatment by the magis- trate, Mr. Newton, as already reported.—Mr. Wontnor post- poned the cross-examination.—Madame Bowman. dress- maker. Southampton-row. deposed that she engaged Mies Cass as forewoman, in the beginning of June. She slept with witness's niece, and was always diligent and very trustworthy.—Two constables then gave evidence as to what °centred at the police station.—lnspector Wyborre said that Endacott_ WAS a zealoue officer. and had brought . .

good many cases of this description.—Miss CRP', recalled, categoricall3 denied the statements made by Endacott at the police court.—Mr. Wontnrr asked for ten day's adjourn- ment; and Mr. Grain said he was in the bands of the court. —lt was then agreed that the inquiry should be adjourned. until Thursday week, and if necessary continued on the following day. MEDLEY'S pamplet " Fair Trade Unmasked,"' Miss Cass has given evidence in the inquiry published by Niessrs. CASSELL and Co. 'Mr- which is being instituted, and she has made GLADSTOIVE, in a recent speech, said that, an excellent impression as a modest respect- notwithstanding the depression in trade, we had able young, woman. It seems that she fainted during recent years.been adding no less than on being taken into the Police Court, and no roo millions per year to the national wealth ; wonder. The night of the Jubilee was to her and in the Report of the Royal Commission a night of horrors on the Depression in Trade and Industry it is given in evidence— "That in recent years, and more particularly in the years during which the depression of trade has pre- vailed, the production of cJinmodities generally. and the accumulation of capital in this count] y, has been proceeding at a rate more rapid than the in- crease of population; while, as regards our foreign trade, the apparent falling off of late years is almost entirely due to the fall in prices which has been in progress since 1873, and more particularly to the fall in the prices of raw materials.'" Agriculture is Suffering in this cairn try: but the rerpedy is to be found not in restor- ing the Corn Laws—not in increasing the price of bread—but in a radical reform of the land laws. The bulk of the land in this coun- try is tied up by settlements, and by the laws of entail and primogeniture, in such a way that it caiihot possibly be put to the best use. There are millions of acres undrained or in- differently drained that cannot be brought into proper condition because the nominal owners, having a life interest only in the soil, take every penny they can get, and spend little or nothing in return. There is, too, the lord of many acres, the whole of whose estates must descend to his eldest son, and who must, by hook or crook. make provision for his younger children. There is, it is true, a good deal of plunder to be had in Church and State for young sprigs of the aristocracy; but thes-t out-door paupers are increasing, competition is getting keener, and .to have something to leave them, money must be got out of the land rather than spent upon it. And thus it is that the land starves, and the people on it starve, and the aristocracy are driven to their wits' end, and all because of insane pride in big estates, and insane laws which tend to keep them biz. Lord DERBY once said that if the land of this country wete brought into proper cultivation, the pro. duct of the soil could be doubled. And who are they, it should be asked. who keep it from being properly cultivated ? Not the strug- gling tenant farmers, who are hampered when they should be helped ; not .the patient hinds whose miserable pittance does not enable them to do more than keep body and soul together; but the landlords of the Fair Trade order who 'block the way for reform, and go mooning after a remedy where no remedy is to be round. If the land of this country were set free, as it is in the United States, and in some countries on the Conti- nent, there would be an immediate demand for the class of labour which is now finding its way into towns, and increasing the struggle for existence. The ordinary labour market would be relieved, the land would be put to its best use. the national wealth would be in- creased, and the " Association for the Pre- servation of Agriculture and our other Indus- tries" would be laughed out of existence.

Sir George Trevelyan is to take the seat at Glasgow which is being vacated by Mr. E. R. Russell. This will be a double gain; it will be a gain to Parliament to have Sir George in the House of Commons, and it will be a gain to journalism for Mr. Russell to return to the editorial chair of the " Liver- pool Daily Post."

The St. Helens Swimming Club have ap- plied for the exclusive use of the Public Baths for one hour per week. This doe § not seem much to ask for, but it is a dangerou3 game to make fish of one and flesh of another in the use of public institutions. There was a lively debate on that subject in the Health Committee; and in the end the application was rejected by five votes to three. •

It is a pity the Vv'atrington Library Com- mittee did not kick in a similar way against the original proposal to break the law, and deal exclusively with the books of the rate- payers by fixing a charge for their use, in addition to the rate of a penny in the pound. It has opened the door to various irregu- larities, and practically shut off the bulk of the inhabitants from the right use of the institution. How long has this illegality to last?

There were some people who were too clever by half in rushing to a conclusion as to the cause of the explosion at the works of Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Co., Cornbrook. The investigation is anything bat a simple one, and has necessitated another adjourn- ment of the inquest. Colonel Majendie would not have asked for further time to continue his inquiries if the cause of the explosion was of a self evident kind.

The Irish Land Bill pleases nobody. Even Mr. Chamberlain is for throwing over the bankruptcy clauses of which he is the reputed author. Now, if the Government would only cut off the head of the bill, lop its tail, and furnish it with a mew body, it might be worth considering.

Lord Randolph Churchill made a MOSE damaging speech on Thursday evening against the Irish Land Bill. He turned it inside out, and showed that it would have to be amended here, there, and everywhere to render it acceptable. The squalls for which we have been looking for some time are coming. If the Government are prepared to make fools of themselves by allowing the Bill to be altered—all except the word •• wherqas "—they may continue to hold office; if not, they will be turned out.

THE Liberal party have attained a victory at Coventry, thus adding to the evidence of other elections that Home Rale principles I are in the ascendant, and that the country has had enough of the present Government. I In this case the Tories are utterly at a lossl to account for their defeat, except by ad- mitting that they are losing the confidence of the electors. Lord SALISBURY chose his battle-field by raising the sitting member for Coventry to the peerage, and it is a matter of course to say that he would not have invited a contest on this particular question if he had thought there was any danger of defeat. Colonel EATON, the son of the retired mem- ber, was regarded as the best possible can- didate that the Tories could bring forward.; and yet he has been beaten. At the last General Election, the Tory candidate was re- turned by a majority of 405 : on Saturday he was in a minority of 16. The contest has been a hard-fought one; for the Tories have managed to add IZ to their total of last year; but the Liberals have added 433 All this goes to show that the out-and-out Liberal , Unionists do not count for much. Those who were so extreme as to vote Tory at the last election will, in all likelihood, have voted Tory again; but their number is small, it would appear, compared with the number of those who, distracted by the , division in the ranks of the Liberal party, ; abstained last year from going to the poll. ' Electors of this class might have some doubts , as to some features of the Home Rule Bill ; I but it is another thing with them when the only alternative that is offered them is an ever-and-ever Coercion Bill. They perceive ! that there can be no settlement of the Irish question by moving in that direction; and i they now see, too, after leisurely examina- tion, that Home Rule is not a very terrible ' thing after all. The Tories are bewildered at the turn of events; the outlook is so much ! I different from what their fancy painted it. They have shouted themselves hoarse in favour of Union ; they have gone black in , the face in denouncing the Nationalists; and it all counts for nothing and less than ; nothing ; for observant electors, having doubts ! as to their sincerity, have begun to regard them as political quacks. The Liberal Unionists are not happy either; they have I been preparing the electors, in their way, I for signs of a spread of "Unionist princi- ples "—whatever the phrase may mean—and when the test is applied it is found that their followers are growing beautifully less. And so it has come to pass that the Tories and the Liberal Unionists are not quite so frater- nal as they were. It is recognised that Mr: GOSCHEN, as " the missing link," does not bind the two parties into one harmonious I whole, and there is talk of reconstruction of ! the Government. But reconstruction won't do; Toryism by another name is Toryism I still. The country has had enough of it; it lwants to go forward; it wants to see the , business of the nation done in a business- like way: it wants to see Mr. GLADSIONE in power again. This, large writ, is the moral lof the recent elections.

What a fuss certain people are Making be- cause European Governments think fit to let us have sugar at less than cost price. There are only about 5,000 workmen engaged in England in sugar refining; but the loss to this country would be over two millions sterl- ing, if, to oblige the 5,000, a countervailing duty were imposed of one farthing per pound. It would pay better to give the 5,000 £2 per week to do nothing.

We have now•a-days Rose Queens as well as May Queens. And why not? The rose is the national flower. and when roses blow the weather is as a rule warm and bright. At Lowton and at Wargrave there was a Rose Queen crowned on Saturday. There is plea- sure to be got out of roses whilst they last. As Herrick has it :
Gather ye rose-buds while ye may, Old Time is still a-flying, And this same flower that smiles to-day To-morrow will be dying.

Lloyd Snape has gained the degree of D.Sc. at the recent examination of the London Unive^sity. Dr. Lloyd Snape is the son of Mr. Thomas Snape, of Widnes, and is the first student from Liverpool who has succeeded in pass- ing the London D.Sc. examination in chemistry. He is one of the "old boys" of the Liverpool Institute, where he received his early education, and where he attained many scholastic distinctions. From thence he entered the laboratory of Dr. Campbell Brown, and studied at University College—at which he was appointed the first demonstrator of chem- istry—subsequently continuing his studies at the Universities of Berlin and Gottingen, under Pro- fessors Hoffmann and Victor Meyer. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT WESTON POINT.—A fatal acci- dent of a shocking character occurred at Weston Point on Saturday aftermoon. A tug commenced to tow the Dutch Galiot "Fides," of Amsterdam, towards Liverpool, but bad not proceeded far upon the journey when the hawser con- necting the two boats gave way. The "Fides" at once cast anchor, end as quickly as possible another rope was procured. When just on the point of getting under weight the mate of the "Fides," named Harm J. De Haan, got his left leg entangled in the tow ropeeand the limb was terribly smashed at the calf. The vessel was put back into Weston Point, but belt an hour was consumed in this opera- tion, and in the meantime the unfortnnate man was bleeding profusely. On arriving at the Docks Captain Clark, the harbour master, took every means possible ta stop the bleeding, and ter. McQougall, of Runcorn, was at once summoned. That gentlemau remained with the injured man for a considerable period, and then obtained assis- tance. It was necessary that the limb should be ampu- tated, bet the man was suffering in severely from the shock to the system and from his low condition that the opera- tion could not be performed. The poor fellow died at Circe O'clock on Sunday morning. The son of the deceased, who is cook on board the " Fides," was a witness of the sad accident. On Monday evening Mr. J. E. Worsley. the coroner, held an inquest en the body, and a jury recorded a verdict of "Accidental death."

The new line will connect St. Hel,ins with Liverpool, S3uthport, and Preston in one direction: and with Manchester and ‘Vigan; and with the dis- tricts served by the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lin- colnshire, the Great Northern, and the Midland Rai/ways, in addition to the extensive system worked by the Cheshire Lines Co•"arnittee.. It has been decided to offer any balance of capital required for public subscription during the last week of September next. The first sod will be cut in the month fol- lowing, and the ceremony, we understand, will bej ! performed by Lord Derby. Lord Gerard of Bryn and ! Mr. W. J. Legh, of Lyme Park, Cheshire, have re- I cently joined the board of directors, of which Mr. j Seton-Karr, M.P., is the chairman.

THE CORNBROOK EXPLOSION.—The adjourned in- quest upon the body of James Martin, who was killed at the explosion which occurred at the , chemical works of Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Co., Cornbrook, on June 2nd, was held on Thursday morning, at the City Coroner's Court, Manchester, before Mr. Sidney Smelt, the Deputy City Coroner. Mr. S'ington appeared for Mr. John Wainwright, an owner of property damaged by the explosion. Mr. Yates appeared for Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Co. The Coroner said he had to tell the jury that Colonel Majendie was not yet quite ready with his I report. The investigation necessitated a good many experiments which were not yet completed. This was a very serious and a very important in- quiry—important to the public and to Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Co., so that there should be no hurry and no haste about it. He (the coroner) was , quite certain that Colonel Majendie was very 1 anxious to get to the bottom of this affair, and to I hurry would be to waste time in so important an investigation. Colonel Majendie had suggested two days in the beginning of August, when he would be ready with his report. Mr. R. S. Dale, the chemist of the firm, was examined as to the nature and quantity of the chemicals in the works at the time of the explosion. He said the explosion was still a mystery to him, and he could not offer the least , suggestion towards an explanation. One fact elici- ted in the examination was that there was some 13 cwt. of picric acid in the section of the works where i the explosion took place, of which nothing could afterwards be found. The inquiry was adjourned till the 4th August,when Colonel Majendie is to ; present his report.
