div.head: BAZAAR AT FRODSFIAM.
div.p: BAZAAR AT FRODSFIAM.

I On Thursday a very successful bazaar, which was held in aid of the benefice of St. John the Evan- gelist, Kingsley, was opened at Belle Mont, Overton Hills, by Mr. Henry .1. Tellemache, M.P. for the Eddisbury division of Cheshire. The weather, though rather threatening in the earlier part of the day, turned out to be beautifuily fine, and there was a good attendance at the opening ceremony. Amongst those present, in addition to Mr. Tolle- mache, were the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, vicar of Kingsley; the Rev. H. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham ; Colonel Ashton, Dr. Steele; Mrs. Heron. Mrs. Ashton, Mrs. Walker, Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P., the Misses Wright, Rev. R. Douglas, vicar Kidsgrove, and Mrs. Douglas, Miss Davies, Mrs. Lewis, &c.—ln declaring the bazaar open, Mr. Tollemache said that he had great pleasure in taking part in the day's pro- ceedings. In the first place he should like to say that it was a great pleasure to him to be able to ac- cept the compliment they had been good enough to pay him in asking him to be present, and it WAS- a great pleasure and satisfaction to him to be able to contribute, in however small a manner, towards the good cause that bazaar had at heart, that was, the increase of the stipend of those who were doing God's work in the neighbourhood of Kingsley. In addition he should like to say that it was a pleasure to him to see so many ot his friends and neighbours. On ordinary occasions, when he had been in the neighbourhood of Kingsley, it had not been on equally favourable and Nippy terms. It was an additional pleasure to come down there when they might all meet without asking any question except the one, "How can we make the bazaar a success ?" Mr. Reynolds had asked him to speak of the object of the bazaar which, he had no doubt, they would be better acquainted with than he was. They had heard a great deal in recent years of the apathetic con- dition of the 'church, how little it was doing. how it neglec- ted its opportunities, but he was glad to think that in the last few years there bad been a great and A welcome change in this matter, that•the church was asserting herself, and was endeavouring to take a stronger position, and to do her duty perhaps better than it had been done in former yea-s. He looked on the day previous through a book which gave all that had been done by the church of late years, and be found that for the object they now bad in view, ..ryl far church extension, building, restoration, &c, during tLe year 1885 there 'vas no less a sum contributed than £1,733,000, and tbat altogether for church purpos-s, not including the item mentioned, there bad been soniething like £18,000,000 contributed. He thought that that was a very healthy and a very favourable si.m, and he Wq• eX. trE tnely glad that an effort was being made in that district to improve the position of Kingsley Chureh. lie was trod that the value of the benefice was only 190 gress value, and out of that sum £65 was deducted to pay off a gen- tleman who for mane' years worked in Kingsley parish, and who now was retired-. The obi r*t of Kingsley parish was to raise £750, which, with additional promises from the patrons of the living, Christ Church, Oxford,woold iner-ve • the stipend of Kingsley Church by something like £lOO a year. He believed premises had been obtained 4 £450. and he hoped sincerely that the result of the bazaar w,fi'd be that a very large proportion of the sum vet ',golfed would be raised. Re was dslightod to hear from Mr. Reynolds how everyone in the parish of Kingsley had worked hard to secure the object which they had in view. There had been DO question of what religieue_denomina.tion _ _ _

the parishiOners-beUnged to, but they la'asd all vrorlied.hard and loyally to promote that noble object. He had very great pleasure in declariag the bazaar open. He had honed to have been able to stay there sometime, and to see a nom- ber of his friends, but the time of a wretched member of Parliament was in no sense his own, and when he came away from London that morning, it was on the expre<s terms that be should be back again at nine o'clock. that night—The sale was then proceeded with. The arr,Ange. ments for holding the bazaar, which were very successfully carried out, were in the hands of the following corrirni've : —Dr Steele, Messrs Joseph Hall. George Parkinson Thomas eirard, Joseph Tickle,E J Walker, William Horton, John Hall, Samuel Lewis, C rE Hitchen, George Jack- son Rev A P Reynolds (vicar), Messrs C D PAlnson (bon sec), and E G Stewart (hon treas.) The principal stallbulders were :—Vicarage st,W lafesdamek A P Reynolds, Steele, T Hewson' C Hewson, Jackson' S Anderson, and the Misses A Steels and IrSteele; Castle Hill utah ;Mrs Walker (Castle Hill), and the Misses Harrison, Lloyd (Chester), and Douglas ; refreshment stall : Mesdames Thomas. Heywood, Turnbull, and Charley; dairy stall : Miss Wilding and Miss Tickle Frodsbam stall : Mrs Puns- ford, and the Misaes Malleson, Croafield, and Simpsan •, old woman's shoe: Mrs Ashton, the Misses Hilditcb. and Miss Whinnerah ; Kingsley stall: Mesdames Horton. Parkinson, Hall, and Gerard, and Misses Okell, Parkbran, IVarb"t9l:l' Mein, Hall, and Gerard; linen gen me Parkinson : flower stall: Mr Hall (Kingsley) • and Mrs Lett Many of the plants bad been supplied by Mr Owen,- of .liart- ford. The stalls were well stocked with miacellaneons articles, many of which were of considerable value. In 'addition to the stalls there was a nilea nond," under the superintendence of Messrs. George Janksan and J. G. Parkinson, and an art gallery in charts! of Mr. R. Holland. Amongst the other attractions provided were the ertisr- tainments of Professor de Mare and Mr. W. R. Duncan. The band of the Indefatigable Training Ship played a selection of music on the opening day. The sale Wat! rrintinued yesterday, and will be again continued to-day (Saturday), , when music will be provided by the Frodsham Clautch , Band.

WIFE AssAneT.—Elijah Bradburn was summoned by his wife Betsy Anne for assaulting her on the Thursday night previous.—Complainant said that on the occasion mentioned prisoner came home drunk, and turned her eat of the house. She went back, and he again turned her oat, and ths oc- curred several times. He also struck her. Witness also told the magistrates that her husband had not given he a shilling for years; she maintained herself and children by keeping a shop. The complainant wished for a separation order to be granted, but the magistrates sent her husband to prison for a fortnight. AN OLD OFFENDER.—EBZiheth Ball, a venerable looking woman, was broueht up on a charge of begging in Church- street.—Prisoner : I am going in 83.—Alderman Burgess: I am very glad to hear it; you are getting nearer the end!— It was stated that prisoner bad been several times before the magistrates, and had been let off three or four times.— Alderman Burgess: She has been many a time at my place begging, and has abused me without measure. We do not (to prisoner) need to pass a severe sentence upon you, be- cause yeu are sure to be either at this court or some other as 9000 as you come out of jail, and you will get another term. You will get fourteen days this time, and if you will keep out of Warrington we shall be much obliged -- Themes Hsrrison, for begging was also sent to prison for a fCTroight. THEFT FROM THE BATHS.—LaWrenCe Spencer, a lad, was charged with stealing a pair of shees belonging to Robert Bradley. another lad, while at the baths in Legh-street, on the afternoon previous—The theft was admitted, but the father of the lad said that he was scarcely responsible for his actions. as he had been somewl,at affected in his mind for some time in consequence of his having fallen off a house and injured himself—The magistrates allowed the lad to go, hot recorded a conviction aeainst him. ATTEMPTED FALSE PRETENCES —Jesse Ditchfield, a gar- dener, was charged with having been found on the premises of Mr. Richard 80117011, 35, Wilson-Patten-street, on the evening previous, for the purpose of endeavouring to obtain money by false pretences. Prisoner represented that he had a valuable contignment of plans that had come from Mold, at Lymm station, but he had not money with which to get them forwarded to Warrington. He therefore sought assist- ance. As he was leaving the back premises of the house of Mr. Powson, he was met by Constable Monaghan, who was watching his movements, and who, by telegraphirg to Lymm, found that the man's story was false.—Ditchfield was sent to prison for a month. Meilen/tee—Before Aldermen Holmes and Harrison, and Councillors J. Pierpoint and Francomb. DRUNEENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Ellen Rabbit, in Buttermarket-street, on Saturday, fined 5s and costs; John Quinn, in Scotland-read, on Saturday, fined 108 and coats; Annie Glassbrook, in Horeemarket-street, on Saturday, fined 5s and costs ; George Goyle, in Pierpoint-street, on the 2nd inst., fined 5s and costs; John Peers. in Horsemarket-street, on Sunday, Seed 10s and coqta ; Thomas Towey and Ann Towey, in Bridge- street, on the 4th inst., the former fined 5s and costs, and the latter ordered to IWO CMOS. DISTURBING THE PEACE.—For this offence John Hewitt and James Arabary were ordered to pay costs, and be boned over in their own recognisances for six months. BAD LANGUAGE —Charlotte Glover, for having used ob- scene and profane language in Mill-lane, on the 3rd inst, was fined 53 and costs. Fnettors DRITING.—Thomas Berry, a young RUM, was summoned for having furiously driven, to the danger of passengers. a horse and luny, in Manchester-road. The case was dismissed. OBSTRUCTIONISTS —The following persons were dealt with for causing obstructions in the streets :—Walter Hat- ton, by allowing a horse and cart to stand an unreasonable time in Market-street, fined 2a 6d and costs; William Mor- timer, by allowing a handcart to remain in Peter-street, ordered to pay 7s costs; Peter Woodward, by allowing a horse and trap to remain in the street, fined 5s including costs; Geo. Harkey, a similar offence, also fined 5s including costs; and John Bush, by allowing ahandeart to remain on the footpath, dismissed. WEIGHING BREAD.—Messrs. Pierpoint and Co., bakers, were summoned for having, on the Bth inst., sold a loaf of bread otherwiee than by weight to George Higham, who had been sent to porehase the loaf by Inspector Place. Mr. J. L. Whittle, depute town clerk, prosecuted on behalf ef the Corporation. Evidence was given to the effect that Higham purchased a 41b loaf, which was served to him without being weighed. Afterwards, when weighed, it was found to be two ounces light. Mr. Whittle did not wish to press the case, as, he said, the offence might have been committed inadvertently, as Mr. Pierpoint, in conse- quence of the serious illness of his wife, was absent at the time. The Bench made an order for the payment of 109 lid, the costs. TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton, Councillors J. Green- ing and J. Pierpolnt, and Mr. E. J. Guest. ' MISCELLANEOUS.— Charlotte Barton, charged with , vagrancy, was dismissed with a caution.—Frederick Wm. Rorke, a deserter from Salford, was remanded to await escort. A NUISANCE —Joseph Smith, house agent, was summoned for permitting a nuisance to exist at the rear of houses in Dallam-lane.—Mr. A. Browne defended.—The Bench directed that the nuisance must be abated, and that the defendant must pay costs. THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. TILL ROBBERY—James Murray (60), a journeyman shoemaker, of Dublin, was chanted with having on the day previous stolen 4s from the shop till of John Hough. shoe- maker, 26, Dallam-lane. He pleaded guilty, and was sent to prison for a month. THEFT BY Boys—Patrick Sauce (12), 15, Town Hill, and Peter Harper (15), 29, Town Hill, pleaded guilty to stealing two cricket balls, value 59, from the shop door of Messrs. Skelton, Horsemarket-street, on the previous day. Sauce was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod, and Harper to receive 12 strokes. DRUNKENNESS.—Daniel Crosby was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Market-place, on the night previous.—lt transpired that he was only realeased from prison on the morning previous, and he begged hard to be let off. —Chief Constable Hunt interceded for the prisoner, and the magistrates discharged him with a elution. FRIDAY.—Bef ore Mr. John White and Dr. Gornall. DRUNKEN/SESS.—Thomas Walsh, for having been drunk in Cloth Hall-yard the same morning, was fined 5s and

costs. TEEFE o Wool3.—William Hibbert was charged with having stolen, on the Bth inst, two pieces of wood, value 6.1, the property of the Cheshire Lines Committee. Defen- dant was in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee as a striker, and on the day in question, at noon, P.C. Williams, of the' Borough Force, observed him to put some- thing over the wall at the works in Battersby-lane. It was afterwards discovered that defendant had taken two pieces of deal which belonged to the committee. It wat stated that defendant had been two years in the employ of the committee, and there had not previously been any complaint against him.—He was fined Ll, inclndinie costs. TIIE MOTHER-IN-LAW.—Edward Weave was summoned by his wife Ellen 1 who complained that be had deserted her. Mr. P. Davies defended. Complainant said that she had been married to defendant for seventeen months. Last Tuesday and the Tuesday previous, he turned her out, and had ill-used her and her mother ever since Che marriage. He in i t a loaded gun n the mom, and she dare not live , with him. Tho defence was that defendant objected to the 11 visits of his wife's mother, about which all the trouble had I af sem Defendant said that his wife's mother was a regular ' jubilee mother-in-law. (Laughter.) He was quite willing to take his wife in, if she would promise that her mother should not visit them. Complainant absolutely refused to again live with her, and the magistrates' clerk said in that case she could not charge her husband with desertion. The case was therefore dismissed. ASSA-CLT CASF.S.—James Bibby summoned Kate Bottom- ley forassaniting him on the 4th inst. She was bound over in her huebaud's reccguizances of £lO to keep the peace for six months,—Elizabeth Patchett and Kate Weedall were summoned for baying assalted Dinah Gleave on the 7th inst. Weedall was dismissed, and Patchett was ordered to find a surety in £lO for her good behaviour for the next six i months, or, n default, to go to prison for a month.-Jane Ashton was summoned by William Sixsmith for having as- saulted him. Mr. U. .1. Longton appeared for the com- plainant. The conflict of evidence was so great that the maglexates dismissed the case.

Stanton.

MAINTENANCE OF PARENTS.—An order to pay is par week towards the maintenance of his wife in a lunatic asylum was made against John Ackerley. and a similar order to pay 3s 61 per week towards the maintenance of his mother in a lunatic asylum wee made against John Simp- son.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. Two persons named Thomas Henry Barton and Joseph Brazen&le were before the court for not having sent their children regularly to school.— Both cases were adjourned. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A NIMALS.—Joseph Quinn, of Dunham, was charged with being the owner of a horse which had been cruelly ill-treated at Lymm, on the 2nd June.—lt was stated by Sergeant Bosons that defendant was the owner of a horse in respect of which a man had been fined at the previoas sessions for letting it out "for a penny a ride."—lnspector Aplin, of the R.S.P.C.A., also gave evidence as to the condition of the horse, and a fine of lOs and costs was imposed,--James Simpsom, farmer, Heatlev, was charged with having caused a horse to be worked whilst in an unfit sitate.—Ha WAS represented by Mr. Hockin, solicitor, Manchester. For the prosecution Joseph Lawson, Inspector Aplin, and Sergeant Bossons gave evi- dence, but ultimately the case was dismissed. 800 CASES.—Arthur Greaves Banning was fined Is and costs for having allowed a dog to be at large at Lvmm on the 4th of June ; John Forster was fined a like amount for a similar offence ; and John Brierlev was dismissed. GAMBLING —Five lads, named Hedlev Clayton, William Jackaon, John Percival, William Rowell, and Thomas Lee were summoned for gambling by playing at cards for money at Newfield. Rich of the youths WAS ordered to pay 2s 13. j. and was warnad by the Bench against appearing again. I MiscErt.ANEors.—George Harrison was summoned for furious driving at Lymm on the 10th inst ; the case was dismissed.--John Platt, for baying been drunk and dis- orderly, at Lymm, on the 29th May, was fined 108 6d and costs, or, in default, fourteen days.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL

In the House of Lords, on Monday, the Manches- ter Ship Ja.nal (Preference Shares) Bill was read a third time, without opposition, and passed. We have great pleasure in announcing that by noon on Wednesday the deposit of £2 per share on £3,000,000 of ordinary capital had been paid into the bank at St. James's Hall, Manchester. The directors are therefore now able to issue the £4,000,000 of preference shares. On Monday night there remained a balance of £28,000 to be paid be- fore the necessary total was reached. On the follow- ing day that balance was reduced by £14,322; and on Wednesday morning the remainder was paid in. There are still a large number of ordinary shares to be issued, and the directors are sitting daily to deal with new applications. The shares of the railway companies affected by the Ship Canal scheme suffered a considerable fall on the London Stock Exchange on Wednesday— Lancashire and Yorkshire declining as much as 2. Subscriptions, it is believed, will be invited for the Manchester Ship Canal Company's preference capital on Tuesday next, Messrs. Rothschild to receive them as before. Interest at the rate of 4 per cent, will be paid during construction, and 5 per cent. after. The whole issue is understood to have been underwritten.

" Cassell's Magazine" for July has a summer look with it. The frontispiece is a bright picture of a young lady—a Rose Queen—gathering roses. It is an illustration of some verse," Blush roses" by Geo. Weatherley. Those who are thinking of "The merchant service as a profession" cannot do better than turn to a valuable article on the subject in this number. The Family Doctor has a chat on Heart Disease, and is, as usual, as pleasant as he is sensible. lipre is a paper, too, about wigs, by Dr. Robinson ; strirne lines (illustrated) on Midsummer, and Chit-chat on Dress, The stories, serial and completed, keep up their interest, "The love-tale of Japan" being Un- commonly good. It is a matter of course to say that The gatherer" has much that is useful in his record of invention and discovery. "The Quiver" frontispiece is also the picture of a lady gathering flowers. " Small 'Beginnings," by Professor Blaigie, should be read by all desirous of helping their fellows in the world ; it is a stimula- ting article. "The Way to Paradise" is a capital story in one chapter ; "Rose Windows" (illustrated) gives an account of some of the finest windows of our cathedrals. The Rev. Dr. Payne Smith has a third paper on " How God preserved the Bible" ; and Mr. H. Gordon Cumming has a paper on" Divining Rods, Ancient and Moderr." "The Short Arrows" are poin- ted, and well illustrated, and there are other interest- ing papers. "Little Folks," for July, is particularly strong. The part forms the commencement of a now volume, and contains the opening chapters of two new serial stories, viz., "Aunt Clcthilda's Guests," by Mrs Molesworth, author of "Carrots," &c., and "The Boy Hunters of Kentucky," by Edward S. Ellis. The specimens of Work shown on pages 37-48, in connection with the Children's Celebration of the Queen's Jubiloe, are especially interesting. "The Magazine of Art" for July opens this week with a very fine etching of Jose Domingo's painting, "Here's to your health." We have the second part of a thoughtful artieleon Current Art, with several delight- ful illustrations. Fernley Hall, which is a storehouse of Turner's works, has justice done to it alike in letter- press and engraving. The reproduction of Turner's " Dort " makes one long to see the original. "Some portraits of Great and Little Masters" has an interest of its own; and there is a capital article, capitally illustrated, on The Salon." "There Ever-shifting Home" is a copy of a painting of great power in this year's Academy. " Random Reminiscences of a Special Artist" is the title of a lively article by Harry Fur- ness, with some exceedingly lively illustrations. There are some fine views of "Australian Coast Scenery," and the usual " Record of Art in June."

"The Lady's World" has the merit as a magazine of fashion and society, of interesting both sexes. The fashion plates may, for the most part be taken 88 types of beauty of the women of different countries. The beautiful coloured frontispiece "A Daughter of Summer "—is a charming type of the English lady, while the Frenchwomen is illustrated in the "Even- ing toilette designed by Worth," and the Austrian in the Society Types, and in the "Summer costume from the house of J. and E. Spitzer, Vienna." Amongst other articles, the contents include Dramatic Notes, Ladies of Note, Artistic Homes and How to Make Them, Summer Health Reiorts, and the Art of Giving Dinners.

" Cassell's Illustrated Shakespeare" reaches part 13 ; it finishes "All's well that ends well " ; and com- mences "Twelfth Night, or What you Will." Part 42 of the Encyclopcedic Dictionary brings the student to the letter I ; the work continues to reveal itself as a marvel for fulness and accuracy. In the current issue of "Familiar Wild Flowers" we have for the first coloured plate the yellow horned poppy, and for the second lady's-smock, bitter-cress or cuckoo-flower. The current number of "The life and times of Queen Victoria" brings the reader up to 1861, and covers the interesting but melancholy period of the death of the Prince Consort. The issue of " Glean- ings from Popular Authors" nears its end; it will make a splendid volume both for text and illus- tration. .

Bowles, Lamb, and llartley Coleridge—three of the minor poets— are included in the issue for this month of the Canterbury Poets, published by Mr. Walter Scott. It is a treat to get the poems of the three in cue shilling volume. Bowles had a large influence in his time which was wholly of a healthy kind. Lamb won immortality in prose; but his verse is also well worth studying. Hartley Coleridge is a sweet singer, and some of his sonnets are nigh perfection. The one commencing— What was't awakened first the untried ear Of that sole man who was all human kind? has secured a world wide fame.

" The Natural History of Selborne," by Gilbert White, reaches U 8 from the same firm as one of the Camelot Classics. It is a book which should be read and re-read in these days of hurry and worry, for it shows bow much solid enjoyment may be ob- tained by patiently watching the world around us. There is no one so badly situated that he cannot fol- low in White's steps in one direction or another, and it is safe to say that, if he does follow him, he will come back refreshed in body and mind. In the Great Writers' series published by Mr. Wal- ter Scott, we have, for July, the "Life of Charlotte Bronte, by Augustine Birrell." This life of the great novelist depends mainly as to material on Mrs. Gaskell's work; but there is a considerable amount of new matter, especially as to Charlotte Bronte's father. Mr. Birrell is not lacking in criticism, and, as he is in sympathy with his subject, he brings out in full relief the finest features of the novels and the novelist. The book is a welcome addition to the series, for Charlotte lironte was undoubtedly a great writer, and the story of her life is therefore well worth telling. "The Westminster Review" for July opens with a carefully prepared article on "The reorganisation of the Liberal party." It summarises the faults of the present system, shows how and why the present or- ganisation is unreliable, and proceeds to suggest re- me4ies. It should be carefully considered by party leaders. "American Education," by a teacher, points the moral of the necessity of teaching children in our day schools with ;complete immunity from sectarian teaching. Other papers are on military and naval administration, Dells Sedie's art of singing, a flitting ghost, Madame Mohl, Persia. a study in religious evo- lution, the federation of the British Empire, and con- temporary literature. .

The July issue of "Scribner's Magazine" compares favourably with any of its predecessors. There is a further instalment of the "Unpublished Letters of Thackeray," with fac-simile of a letter and drawings; and a continuation of the "Illustrations of Napolean and his times." Dr. D. A. Sargent contributes a paper on the physical proportions of the typical man, with illustrations and diagrams of a most interesting kind. "A girl's life eighty years ago," is capital reading; it forms a bright picture of the past. The continued stories increase in interest, and the poetry is much above the average. "The English Illustrated Magazine" still holds its own admirably as a sixpenny publication. "Chatter" is the title of the frontispiece ; it is engraved from a drawing by Herbert Gandy. "Old Hook scud Crook," by Basil Field. is a bit of pleasant reading. It is illustrated by H. Thompson. whose clever character drawings have proved one of the best features of this magazine. "Walks in the Wheatfields," and "The private journal of a French mariner" are alsonppro- priatelv illustrated. Part 9 of the revised and enlarged History of Lan- cashire, published by Mr. John Heywood, is exceed- ingly interesting. It gives in fac-simile the letter to Lord Monteagle. which resulted in the discovery of the Gunpowder Plot. There is an account of witch craft in Lancashire—the details which famished the basis of the story of the Lancashire witches—and there is a fine view of Hoghton Tower with an account of King James's visit to Lancashire. "The early work of George Cruikshank " is the title of the leading paper of "The Manchester Quar- terly." It is illustrated, and is from the pen of Mr. 11. Thornber, who has evidently made Crinkshank a close study. The frontispiece of the magazine is a reproduction of Cruikshank's famous picture of the massacre of Peterloo in 1819. Mr. H. A. Howarth, M.P., furnishes a raper on " Pythagoros and India," and Mr. Richard Hooke has a very readable sketch, "The Devil's Well. Other papers are "the subjective theory of Beauty," by Mr. R. Barber; "Hand Shakes," by Mr. W. I. Wild; "By the Swab," by Mr. John Mortimer; and "The Wood" by Mr. W. E. A. Axon.

Ward and Lock's Technical Journal and Industrial Self •Initructor (part 32) contains papers for brick• layers, carpenters, the maehiah makers, gardeners farmers, cabinet makers, road makers, land drainers, croziers ; and there is besides a cyclopcedic technical dictionary. It should be stated that the various articles are profusely illustrated. "The Moniteur de la Mode (le.) is to hand with 100 illustrations and four coloured plates. The con- tents for the current month include review of Paris f ishions, musical chit-chat, children's i•lress in Lon- don and Paris, health, and beauty. Sporting cos- tumes, fashionable needlework, &c. It is published by Messrs Myra and Song, who also issue " Myra's Jour- nal of Dre•ts and Fashion" (Gd.) and " Myra's Taree- Penny Journal." We have also received Mrs Leech's Practical and Family Dress•maker.

WIMBLEDON RIFLE MEETING. The opening day of this year's meeting was Mon- day, which was one of great variety in weather. The morning broke so doubtfully that the inhabi- tants'of the camp were uncertain whether they were to be grilled or soaked, or whether puggerees or waterproofs were to be the day's wear. The complaints against the wind were latterly loud and deep. and there is no doubt it spoilt by its vagaries many a good score. Two very interesting team matches and one great general competition were the principal features in the programme. One of the matches was that between two teams representing te officers of the Army and the Reserve Forces re- spectively, instituted this year for the purpose of stimulating small bore practice at thelongest ranges with a view to qualifying for such competitions as that for the Elcho Challenge Shield. The teams were each of six officers, who fired fifteen shots at each range. The Auxiliaries, as might be supposed, won the match but by a very narrow majority, con- sidering the amount of the aggregates. Their grand total was 1,061, against 1,049 by the army officers, or a majority of only a dozen points. The other match was for the Ilumphry Cup, between the Uni- versity "fours." at the three longest ranges, with fifteen shots at each. Oxford made 638, against 567 by Cambridge, or a majority of 71. Last year the aggregates were—Oxford 739, and Cambridge 725, a majority ot 14. _ _ _ _

TnE QUEEN AT HATFIELD—On Wsdnesday the Queen for the second time during her reign, paid a visit to the ancient country seat of Lord Salisbury at Hatfield. Her Majesty's former visit was with the Prince Consort in 1846, when she stayed several days, having a soec,al suite of rooms placed at her disposal, which have ever since been known as Queen Victoria's rooms. The Queen left Wind- sor at half-past three in the afternoon, arrived at Hatfield at a quarter to five, The streets of the villiage were gaily ' decorated, and every preparation had been made for her Majrsty's reception at Hatfield House. Lord Salisbury had invited about three hundred distinguished guests, and his lordship's tanantry and numbers of other visitors were ad- mitted to pork grounds by tickets, so as to enable them to see her Majesty. The band of the Royal Engineers was also present, and played selections of music. The Queen was received at Hatfield Station by Lord Salisbury, his brother, Lord Eustace Cecil, and Lord Cranborne. Her Majesty was accompanied by Princess Beatrice, Princess Irene of Hesse, Prince Henry of Battenberg, and Princess Alexandra of Hesse. The Princess of Wales arrived pre- viously. On driving through the park her Majesty was loudly cheered and frequently bowed her acknowledgments. The Queen, after entering the house, proceeded to one of the terraces where she remained for some time, listening to the music and chatting with the Presider and his'guests. Her Majesty afterwards took tea in the house, and left Hatfield Station a few minutes past seven for Windsor, having pre- viously expressed the great satisfaction she had derived ft om the visit.

CREWE ALEXANDRA V. WIDNES CLUB AND GROUND.— On Saturday the Alexandra team journeyed to Widnes to play the return match with the club of that town, who had the assistance of the famous Lancashire player, Jack Briggs Lyon won t`te toss, and sent the home team to the wickets. Briggs and Callon were the first batsmen, the bowling being shared by Fenn and Henshall. Much to the disappoint- ment of the spectators Briggs was caught by Sadler without scoring, off Fenn's first over. On Colquitt joining Callon a stand was made, and not before 30 runs had been scored was Callon bowled by Billington. None of the others gave much trouble, with the exception of Holt and Reay, the Alexandra fielding being very loose indeed, and the inninge closed for a total of 90. The Alexandra commenced batting_ with Lyon and Henehall. Briggs took the first over, in which Lyon was dispoeed of by a catch behind the wickets. On Payne joining ilenshall the score rose rapidly until Henshall was hit on the arm and had to retire. Fenn filled the vacancy, and the score rose to 34 ere Payne was taken at long field off Briggs Price now partnered Fenn, the latter treating the spectators to some brilliant hitting, mak- ing 13 off one over from Briggs. After the dismissal of Fenn, Sadler, Osborne, and Dutton were soon disposed of. Benshall went in again. and he and Price, who was playing splendid cricket, played out time. From the appended scores it will be seen that time was only wanted to add another victory to the list of the Alexandra. Score :

WARRINGTON v. SEFTON.—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday, and, owing to the frequent showers, was left drawn in favoar of the borne team. The home team won the toss, and commenced with J. J. Crosfield and Tinsley, to bowling of Shore and EYRIIB. Rua-getting was extremely difficult, as the bowlers were bowling ex- ceeding well. In the tenth over, Crosfield was cleaned bowled by Shore ; and four overs later Denton was beaten by Evans. Shore got plenty of work on the ball;: but on Bettesworth coming to the wicket when Clarke was bowled, be was unable to dislodge the batsmen. .Bettesworth made a magnificent &ire out of the ground for six, and hit Shore twice for four. Champion bowled vice Shore, and Bettes- worth was caught on the boundary from a lofty drive by Repel.. His hitting was hard and clean and the spectators were evidently delighted with his dashing though careful play. His score (34) included a six, five fours, two couples, and singles. Smith and Podmore aided Tinsley in raising the score to 160, when Tinsley was out for a splendidly played 62. He went in first and was out seventh. not hav- ing given a chance throughout his innings, which included nine fours. Although at the first apparently nonplussed by Shore, he afterwards settled down to a thoroughly good form, and his innings was worthy of the reputation with which he joined the club. The innings closed for 172. Champion was the most succ.ssful bowler, getting four wickets for 44. Raba again stopped play, and the ground, just softened on the top sufficiently to give the ball work and bard underneath, made the bowling kick up greatly. The light was also very bad, and Roper, Champion, and Travis could make no stand again Smith and Tinsley. Three wickets were down for 27: Linsley (pro.), 5 runs, 5 overs, and 4 maidens; R. Yorkshire bad the best of Cheshire at Halifax on Satur- day by an innings and 235 runs. Lee made a splendid innings of 206, which he was four hours in compiling. At Birmingham, on Tuesday. the display of cricket by the Warwickshire batsmen against the Yorkshire bowling was of the weakest character, and the home county were twice got rid of for totals o! 128 and 96, which left Yorkshire winners by an innings and 1.60 runs. At Lord's on Tuesday, in the game between Gentlemen and Players, the former suffered defeat by an innings and 123 runs. The professionals, in their innings, made 396. Briggs carrying out his bat for a freely hit 66. The main cause of the breakdown of the batting was the condition of the ground, but still the players thoroughly earned their success by good all-round cricket. On Tuesday, at Lord's, a meeting was field of the repre- sentatives of cricketine counties to consider the report of the sub-committee which was formed last year to consider the advisability of forming a Cricket Council, to deal with county cricket. Representatives were present from thirteen counties. It was resolved to receive the repert of the sub-committee that a Cricket Council be formed, and that as regards the Paws of cricket, the Council shall have no executive power, that upon all questions raised under the rules of the county nullification, the committee of the hi.C.C. shall adjudicate,•that it be competent for the Coun- cil to alter or amend the rules of county cricket, that the Council co»sist of one representative each from those coun- ties assembled at Lord's in December, 1886. and that a sub- committee of five representatives from the counties of isliddle3ex, Kent, Surrey, Sussext and Gloucestershire be ap- pointed to frame by-laws and report to the Council before the end of the year.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER..
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER..
LONDOH. THURSDAY..

- ----- • Never since the earliest days of the General Elec. tion of 1880, when accumulated returns proclaimed Liberal victory all along the line, has there been such a marvellous change inthe attitude of parties- as has been effected within the past fortnight. Be- fore the Spalding election the Liberals kept a.bold front towards the enemy, but it is no, secret that hope was very faint in their hearts. As long as the unholy. alliance between Radicals and Conservatives was maintained in the House of Commons, so long would Lord Salisbury's Government maintain its supremacy. The alliance has just been put to the most severe test possible.. When men like Mr.. Chamberlain and his immediate followers found it possible to vote for a Coercion Bill, there was ob- viously no limit to• the lengths they *ould g:o in, order to accomplish their avowed purpose of, keep- ing Mr Gladstone out. People on both sides had got into the habit of believing that the• state of parties in the House of Commons represented the' feeling out of doors, an assumption which, if. well ,founded, made-the prospect exceedingly blank. The election at Spalding gave a rough shocksto i this theory, and the elections n North Paddington and Coventry completely dispelled it, It is all very well to talk about bye-elections not supplying re- liable indication of the state of political feeling throughout the country. Here we have three bye- elections completing within themselves as perfect a sample of the bulk as could be selected.. We haye an agricultural county constituency,,a metropolitin constituency, and a busy. borough.; and they have united in giving a verdict against the' Government. Perhaps the' most remarkable and promisingieature in the case is the. total disappearance of the Dis- sentient Liberal. It is angrily complained. of :in Conservative circles, and plaintively admitted in the camp of Lord Hartington' that the Dissentient Liberal did not appear as a factor in either of the three latest electiorts. If the test here variously ap- plied fairly indicates-the state of affairs throughout, the country, there is, a bad quarter' of an hour coming for the sixty or seventy gentlemen who are directly responsible, for-the maintenance in, power, of such a Government as that which holds the reins at present. However the fact be, it is certain that the so-called "Unionists " are shaking in their shoes,, and their allies on the,treasury bench are in a state of :piteous perturbation. On the other side, the Liberals are gull of hope and spirits, a state of things which, acting and reacting, is likely to have some effect on the pending elections,. , Mr. Gladstone was in the House to-night; as has been, at least up to the dinner hour, every night of the week. Looking down upon the Front Bench from the gallery opposite, it struck, me that the veteran leader is the ydtingest and freshest looking man, on the Bench. He has-coine out in full summer "fig," light coat and trousers, white waistcoat, and blue tie. Summer weather and sum- mer clothing suit him. He always looks well in them, particularly just now.. H'e looks ,tent years younger than he did at any time between 1880 and 1885 when he sat on the Benet' opposite,. and bore the brunt of the venemous opposition of the. now divided Parnellites and Conservatiives. It is &sig- nificant circumstance that quite a long time has elapsed since Air.. Gladstone alluded, to , the prospect of his near departure. This is the less important, as there are gentlemen on the other side, like Colonel Saunderson, who, are readyto,supply the deficiency. The last time Mrs Gladstone alluded to the subject was at Dr. Parker's breakfast—now, a matter of history. He certainly does not look as if he were fading away, and seems, indeed, still fit for ten orfiftedn years hardwork.. , I hear a curious, story about the, Queen and the Women's-Jubilee Fund, which I repeat with the as- surance that it came to me from, a lady whose inti- mate relations with the Court give it much-needed authority.- When the project received her Majesty's approval, it was w, ith the understanding, on her part; that the fund was a personal one, the money to be appropriated for private purposes. Indication of this intention was early given by the-announce- ment that the first purposes to, which the money should be devoted-would be the erection of another statue to, the Prince Consort. It willhe reraembered that the shock created by this announcement was nearly the death of the proposal. It was only upon the assurance that the statue would cost compara- tively, little, and that the balance would be devoted to some worthy public object, that the checked tide of donations, was set flowing again. Whether or not the Queem was permitted to learn what was being said in public 1 don't know; but it is certain that for a long time after, up to within a very recent date, she still entermined the purpose of appropriating the money for personal use, and made no secret of the object to which the money should be devoted. It appears that the Royal Jewel case is deficient in pearls. The Women's Jubilee- offbring seemed a providential means of supplying this deficiency; and the Queen set her heart upon devoting:the balance, after providing for the Prince Consort's statue, to the purchase of a pearl necklace to be the ' finest in the world. When this intention was.com- municated to Lord Salisbury,. he very plainly told the Queen it would not do,, and the intention was reluctantly abandoned. A series of photographs of Mr. Parnell, taken at various periods during the last twelve years, would be as curious as it would, be interesting. Re- has an odd habit of transmogrifying his appearance as far as manipulation of his hair and beard go. One diffi- culty in the way of securing the collection is that Mr. Parnell has almost as great an objection to sit- ting for his portrait as Mr. Disraeli had. it will be noticed that Mr. Tenniet, who is generally so happy in catching the likeness of a public man, always ignominiously fails when he attempts fa! draw Mr. Parnel/. He is, as all artists can, understand, one of those. faces which it is difficult to reproduce by the- art of the pencil.' Oddly enough the, sun, usually unimpeachable as a portrait painter; is baffled by Mr. Parnell's face. I have two portraits which the Irish Leader gave me SOlale years ago, one taken in Washington during his first visit to the United States, and the other without the name of' the artist of the &awn where it was taken. Neither israuchbetter than Mr. Tenniel's efforts in "Punch. They, however, illustrate Mr. Parnell's earlier style of wearing, his hair and beard, both pretty closely trimmed. This is what may be reckoned his third style, and marks an epoch of comparative civilisation. When he first entered Parliament he wore his hair Yong and his beard shaggy. One time, during the height of ob- struction excitement, he amazed the House by pre- senting himself .with the crown of his head shaved and his beard and moustache savagely cropped short: Last year he went back to the earlier style, his hair hanging over his - collar, a la Buffalo Bill. Then it was cut again, and only this week has he turned up in the ll6use with his beard and mous- tache growing wild again, adding to the haggard- ness of his appearance. In addition to this peculi- arity, he wears a brown billyeock hat, the general effect being to suggest the presence of an artist, who, in pursuit of his profession, has been out all night. -

Fthe savage discord now prevailing in political circles has a notable •effect in society. A. lady famous for the political reunions which take place at her house tells me that life has tkcome a burden to her. Once out of a vast list of acquaintances, either in the Tory or the Liberal camp, shewas able to make up a dinner or a luncheon party with the certainty that of her guests each would find himself in pleasant and friendly company. It is one of the best lights of English •politics that the lion of Liberalism will sit down at dinner with the lamb of Toryism, and enjoy the feast all the more from the piquancy of the association. But since what is called "Unionism" has had birth, things are very different. -Men who were formerly inti- mate friends and co-workers are now at daggers drawn, and if by any chance they meet at the

same table a painful and embarrassing silence P veils. Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Labouchere are prominent examples of what has come to p?,se• were formerly, both politically and socially, t closet "chums," constantly interchanging dinner°' and meeting each other at the table of friends. o_.! course no one would now ask the two to meet. Bu" difficulties daily arise in cases of less well-hneyfft ruptures. Lord Randolph Churchill, TAW° ler 'a good deal, is a standing dish of discomfiture. ghosts and hostesses. It would, I expect, be iniPO •sible for him to sit down at any table where well-known people are met without having & nes,,,be .quarrel with two or three of those present.- .10 'number of people he "doesn't speak to is including at at the present time, I believe, eirerY lord pant oi the Treasury Bench. This is a little on the kind people who lay themselves out to ell.teTs tam, and at present there is no prospect of tot' improving. Gbod wine may need no bush. /LT' pictures are all the better fbr good hanWctere• don't think we rightly knew how rc i h „o' oos Gallery hitays Pictures that used to be n dark corners have,,,Thre out with a force and value that shows II?: justly they have been treated. I don't thin" lind one—except a professional grumbler fault with the Blenheim Raphael. It looks gull% superb in its new and deserved position, ete,w/lithe the vista of galleries as you enter the vestibuitetis of new rooms give ample space for some 11,10 oo be° other pictures. Happily people aretaral_ Oore queathing to the nation—a custom rtme —will now popular with the general public than with the appointed heirs.

Sir,—Referring to the r—em—ar—k-s"; the above in your issue of the Otte hest, will you kindly allow space in your paper for a few lines on behalf of the St. Helene Cyclist's Club. The proceedings are viewed by the members of the club with as much regret as by the general public, and we t,ave arranged for a special meetinz of the club to be called for Friday the 22nd just, when a mo3t searchioz. inyastig,ation of the affair will be made, and until this takes place the whole of the prizes offered for this race will be withheld. In the meantime we must ask the public to suspen4 their judgment, as we assure them we wish to put ourselves in a right position towards thern.—Yours truly. CHARLES GOUG}H, Hon. Sec.

div.head: FIRST AID TO THE INJURED.
div.p: FIRST AID TO THE INJURED.

Sir,—l see by paragraphs that have appeared in "The Examiner "that the members of the county police stationed in this neighbourhood are making themselves proficient in the principles of the St. John Ambulance Association. HOW useful is the knowledge that they thus acquire is shown by an occurrence that took place the other week, when one of the constables rendered aid that, in all probability, saved a person's lire. I have not yet heard, however, of any move- ment being made in this direction by the borongh police. There are, no doubt, doctors in Warrington who would take an interest in a St. John's Ambulance Class for the police, and I think that A town like Warrington should not be without one. Of course, I am aware that we hare an ex- cellent infirmary, li,ut in eases of accident first aid of an efficient character saves the injured much suffer ng„ and in many cases proves to be the saving of life.—Yours, O. K. Warrington, July 13, 1887.

div.head: SUGGESTION TO MR. DIGGLE.
div.p: A SUGGESTION TO MR. DIGGLE.

Sir,—As Mr. William Diggle is so fond of making sug- gestions, and airing grievances, in the newspapers, perhaps he will not mind a suggestion being male to him. Accor- ding to him Warrington must be such a very undesirable place to live in that I would suggest that it —ould he a seise thing for him to betake himself to some favo,.red spot more to his liking, and remain there. It would be rather hard on the residents of that particular place, but urely Warring- ton deserves a little rest from William's vagaries, and, now , that the Ship Canal is really' and truly going to be made, the inhabitants will be too busy to attend much to the creakings of persons of that ilk. While on the subject of the canal. shy, let me ask you awl your readers to shout " Hurrah," and likewise Bravo," and to throw up your hats and cheer, for Warrington can now look forward to a run of prosperity that will much astonish the Diggleites. Twice have I heard tha versatile William fling his denunciations at the scheme and its promoters, as he appears to fling them at anything that looks like a suc- cess, but his voice has been unheeded. Diggle preaches, anti Diggle scolds; the publ:c laugh and make merry at his expense. The Ship Canal still progresses on the road to success, and the sanitary arrangements of the borough con. finite to be so admirable as to form an example worth emulating. Mr. Diggle is not " nnderstanded of the people" in these parts. Therefore I would ask him to go hence quickly, or cease to trouble us with his meandering prattle.—Yours, dm, BORED. Warrington, July, 1887.

div.head: HOWLEY INTERCEPTING DEPOT.
div.p: THE HOWLEY INTERCEPTING DEPOT.

Sir,—Since reading the rather alarming letter of Mr. Diggle in your last week's paper with regard to the smell from Howl.y intercepting depot, I have taken the trouble to walk past that intsresting place on two or three occasions to see if my experiences would correspond with those of Mr. Diggle. I must confess that—although not at all prejudiced In favour of the denote, but rather the contrary—l was not a little surprised to find so little smell emanating from the depot. On one occasion the place was in fell operation, and I could hear that the men were at work by the rattling of the tabs which were being emptied and cleaned ; but a few yards away from the building the disagreeable odour was of the faintest description. On another occasion that I Went past the place was closed, and not the faintest smell could be perceived. Speaking for myself, I must say that almost every day I pass private works in the town which give off smells vastly more an- noying than anything I felt at Howley depot. It aeems from his letter that Mr. Diggle has identified the smell from the depot so far away as Church-street, aud if (his is so, he must be congratulated on baying a wonderfully keen and analytical nose. His olfactory nerves must be more acute than was the sense of taste of the two famous wine-tasters,—relatives of Sancho P.anz we read about in "Don Quixote." But really, sir, the very' fact that Mr. Diggle has such a phenomenal nose spells the value of his testimony on this subject. all we can fairly expect the Sanitary Committea to do in this matter is to prevent the depots from becoming offensive to ordinary, people. If a man, who seems to have as keen a 1109 e for a stink as a vulture had to be pleased why a,most every trade except, pefhaps that of the perfumer, would have lobe put a stop to.--Yours, &c., S. M.,
OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. LFROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDRNT. 23, Old Broad-streat, B.C.

The Stock Exchange settlement is just c.impieted and, fortunately, without incident so far as failures are concerned. The general tone of the market is low and depressed, and there is a marked indisposition to enter into fresh transac- tions, especially while foreign politics are in such a state of uncertainty. Bulletins from Pa-is have been carafully scrutinized this afternoon for any sign of the anti-German demonstration which the "Daily News" has led us to expect. In home railways the tendency is downwaid. The rumoured successful issue of the Manchester Canal revival scheme has to sufficient to send down Lancashire and York- shire another while Brighton deferred is down t. The sensational rise in Mexicans of every kind, which has been a feature until the past fortnight, has all but ceased to attract attention. The rise was a little bit genu- ine, and a very great deal artificial, therefore, as is now in- variably the case with artificially induced movements the fall was great. That fall was considerably accelerated by the fact getting abroad that the very people who have been instrumental in forcing the rise were the first to rush into the market and sell. There is, however, every reason to I anticipate a sharp r‘cevery, and speculators who can afford to wait may de very much worse than buy Mexicans to lock up. There is very little doing in the shape of new comp inies. ' The average promoters with a new project ready to launch are painfully susceptible to every influence likely to affect it, and many a promising scheme falls stillborn through this over-cautions dread of being premature. At the present msment there are a dozen or two of companies in this state of nervous expectancy. The reasons assigned by the pro- moters for the delay are varied and amusing. The ap- proaching holiday and the too fine weather, the pausitv of new issues are some of the principal objections against tempting fortune. And perhaps this caution is on the right side this time, for very few of the new companies of the past month have received anything like a reason- able share of public support. There are one or one or two big schemes in embryo. One of the met prom- ising is in the hands of a proved leviathan, who will ask for a quarter of a million to acquire the Rubinat-Condal mineral water property in Spain. This water will be the biggest thing of the day in its line. It is said to be a per- fect cure for liver complaints, on the authority of Dr Merell Mackenzie and Robson Roose. I don't think there is any ,doubt of the public taking that up. The sale of the water will, it is fully anticipated, far ex- ceed the Hunyadi-Janos, which is the nearest approach to Rubinat-Condal in its medicinal properties. The sale of Hunyadi is 17,000,000 annually, and Rubinat-Condal is an- ticipated to reach 25,000,000. A company to acquire the springs and work the business Is being formed with a highly influential board, and under the most favourable auspices, so that its success is already assured.

The South Eastern Railway Company annoonced on Thursday, subject to final audit, a half-yearly dividend at the rate of per cent per annum on the ordinary stock, car- rying forward a4palance of £7.000. The dividend is the same as the corresponding half of last year.

div.head: MR. C.EIAMBF.RLAIN'S CONSTSTENCY.
div.p: MR. C.EIAMBF.RLAIN'S CONSTSTENCY.

Sir,—! was thoroughly taken stack in looking over your correspondence column, i,, to-day's " Examiner," to see no trace of "Fiat Justitia's "reply to my letter of the 2nd inst, and considering that he took the initiative, and invited discussion, really one would have thought he was prepared to have stood his ground, viz., to establish his charge of inconsistency against Mr. Chamberlain in bin Irish policy. But it is very gratifying to us Radical Unionists to find that " Fiat Jastitia's " bold attempt to prove success- ful, where all others before him have ventured but failed, should have failed also. No other course was open to him but failure, and I trust he will have profited, and become a wiser man but at the same time I think it is nothing but fair that I should insist upon "Fiat Juatitia " either ac- knowledging his inability to prove Mr. Chamberlain's incon- sistency, or making a further attempt and prove that I have net made out my case, viz., to show the absurdity of his position. However, be that as it may, if he thinks the wisest course is to be silent, and let his misrepresentations be forgotten, I shall have to tender to you, Mr. Editor, my thanks for permitting me an opportunity of preventing these base misrepresentations being thrust down the throats of I the electorate. There is a maxim with politicians that if you throw a lot of mod, some will sure to stick. I hope this was not the purpose of" Fiat Justitia " considering he terms himself a Liberal, for such motives I have always thought to be foreign to the Liberal party. Well,! suppose that his failure to substantiate his position will not trouble him mtacb, after the result of the bye•elections, the success of which will be short-lived on account of the uncertain position they are in as to the course Mr. Gladstone will take, if (which is unlikely) he is returned to power. I feel confident the Radical Unionists are pursuing the right course, and in the end are bound to be successful, for the simple reason that "Thrice is be armed that bath his quar- rel juat."—l remain, yours respectfully, . RADICAL UNIONIST.

div.head: HOW IS IT?
div.p: HOW IS IT?

Sir,—ln the contention with ikir: Chamberlain over the Irish question, his Radical "unauthorised programme" has been shunted out of notice, and as to his doctrine of " res. titution," that seems Quite forgotten. The abuse from Tory I papers and politicians, however, which encountered him when he uttered this alarming but just principle, ouhgt to have left him straight for all time, and made him shrink from any alliance with the " oppressors " (Mr. Bright's designation) who were the originating cause of such a doc- trine being preached, and on whcm the process of disgorging would have to be carried out. The revelations of heartless rack-renting that have prevailed, and still prevail in Wales as well as in Ireland, amply justify the righteous claims of restitution being set up and pushed home. It is instructive to read a passage in the Tory "Quarterly," even so far back as 1817, which shows compactly bow the process of deple- tion of the fruits of a people's industry, how indeed the system of plunder has been going on so as to satisfy the voracity of landlords. The writer speaks of "ill-regulated , societies," by which he means ill-governed conntriss, from which" exportation may habitually take place while the mass of the people, or the very labourers who produce the surplus provision, are reduced to a degree of poverty and privation comparatively unknown in the countries which are dependent OR them, and which receive the annual sup- ply," i.e., the surplus so-called. "Ireland and Poland have long exported, yet no one who knows the situation of their inhabitants will deny that there is more habitual dis- tress, more squalid poverty endured there, than in their cus- tomers England and Holland. The actual supply of Ireland [in export] consists of the finest pork and beef; but what does this-avail the cotter who is supported on milk and po- tatoes? The actual supply of Poland consists of the finest wheat, but what does this benefit the peasant, whose ordi- nary subsistence is obtained from rye bread and an inferior kitid of pulse ?"—p. 393. Who will say after this, that the good old Hebrew dntrine of restitution is not a righteous one, and should be enforced. But how is it that astates- man, who bad hold of a principle in which the "divine 1 justice "is so grandly exemplitiA, should have flung it aside? Alas, how is it? L.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

ANNIVERSARY SERMONS —SOIMORS were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel, Five Crosses, on Sunday afternoon and evening, by Mr. William Shepherd-Allen, of Woodhead Hall, Staffordshire. when the collections, which were in aid of the Sunday school expenses, amounted to £l4 lb ed. Suitable hymns were sang by the choir.

A FRODSHAM MAN DROWNED AT NORTHWICH.—An in- quest was held at the Bridge Inn, Northwich. on Saturday, before Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, touching the death of Jos. Burithill, aged 22, whose house was at Caurch-street, Fred- sham, wheee body was discovered in the Weaver on Friday morning.—Henry Cornea, waterman, Leftwich, deposed to taking the flat Supply to Winsford on Thursday night, and on board were Davies, the captain, and deceased. Burk. bill formed one of the crew, and Davies told witness that he had taken the deceased, who was a novice in such matters, and that he had given him work on board the flat out of. compassion, he having no other work to do. They went to Winsford for the purpose of loading salt, and having got a cargo on board they returned to North wich, where they arrived at 9 30. About four o'clock in the morning Davies came to him, and asked him if the deceased had been in his berth. Witness said " No." Davies then remarked that the deceased, who had been sleeping with him, got up and went on deck. He thought be heard him come down again, but he did not know exactly whether it was so. for he soon fell asleep agaia. They looked round the vessel for the de- ceased,and felt in the water with boat hooks. Ultimately they got a hook fastened to a piece of ',ape, and dragging the water with this appliance the body of the deceased was I brought to the surface close to the vessel's side. Burkhill had his trousers, shirt, stockings, and waistcoat on.—The Coroner said it WAS purely imaginative how the usan got in the water. lie idea was that going on deck he accidentally slipped overboard. He thought the verdict that it would be proper for the jury to return Was "Accidentally drowned." The jury returned a verdict to this effect.

div.head: RUNCORN BANKRUPTCIES.
div.p: THE RUNCORN BANKRUPTCIES.

Before Mr. Registrar Nicholson, at the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, on Friday, the public examina- tion of Mr. Henry 'Randle, draper, &c., Runcorn, was resumed. On the case being called, Mr. Dibb (the official receiver) stated on a former occasion he pointed out there was a sum of £BOO or £9OO unac- counted for in regard to the accounts presented to the court by the debtor, and the case was adjourned to give the debtor an opportunity of explaining that deficiency. After two or three attempts he had succeeded in doing so. hills first statement the debtor had over estimated the value of his new stock, accounts had been twice entered in the cash book, and other errors in book-keeping had been made. The explanations left the sum of £l9O only practically unaccounted for, and he thought that sum might be explained if the various books were properly worked out. He (the official receiver) thought it would be idle to ask the registrar to make an order directing the bankrupt to be prosecuted, but when the bankrupt applied for his dis- charge it would be his duty to poir,t out that proper books had never been kept, and that an enormous amount of trouble had been given to the court, the trustee, and officials, in getting them something like right.—The Regis- trar remarked that it was obvious the way in which the books and accounts had been kept wat very un- satisfactory, but he did not think there was now a necessity for prosecution, though it struck him in a different light on the former occasion. He had only himself to blame for his neglect and vant of business ability or attention in keeping his books and accqunts.—The Official Receiver remarked that he was told by the trustee that the dividend would only be at the rate of about 3s in the X.—The Regis- trar said the adjournments and subsequent pro- ceedings had necessitated additional expense.—The Official Receiver : It is satisfactory to the credi- tors to know that there has been no fraud or anything of that sort.—The public examination was then closed.

The case of Mr. William Farrell, formerly a builder and ' contractor at Runcorn, was also called. Mr. Dibb (official receiver) stated that at a former meeting he had a lengthened examination into accounts, which were of a very complica- ted character. The liabilities had been filed as £8,559 15s 2d, but by an arrangement with Mr. Kirby the trustee had been able to reducs them by the sum of £.2,783 12s 10d, leaving £5.776 3s 4a. On the other hand, the assets had been increased by the sum of £330, and the deficiency was accounted for in a very reasonable and proper manner. Tile unfortunate portion was the Farnworth estate, with which the bankrupt bad been connected. The cost of the property was £ll,OOO, and the present estimated value only £3,800, leaving £7,200 as the gross loss, which had, however, been amended with the arrangement with Mr. Kirby.—ln reply to the Registrar, the Official Receiver and the Trustee stated they did not think there would be any advantage to the creditors in keeping open the public examination, and it was closed.

Mr. William James Shore, ship chandler, was also sailed up on his- adjourned examination by the Official Receiver. Mr. Rodway (Liverpool), and Mr. P. Davies (Warrington), represented creditors. The Official Receiver cross-examined the bankrupt in reference to cash gifts from his relatives, and the bankrupt admitted that if his accounts and books had been properly balanced and audited be would have seen that his personal expenditure was exceeding his income before he filed his petition. He also said he had not paid over to the owners of ship shares money which had been received on their behalf, amounting to £lso.—The Official Receiver said he would report to the court that that was a breach ot trust. He wished to say that in the first instance he formed a very bad opinion of Mr. Shore, and I felt that as he was a most unsatisfactory man it was his duty to examine into his conduct as much as possible. He felt bound to say that Mr. Shore, from causes which he need not define' had been an enemy to himselt. If he had been frank, and open, and not endeavoured to conceal certain things which he ought not to have concealed he need never have raised the mountain of suspicion which had been raised against h:m. There were oftmces he had committed such as, the want of proper books, Sic , but he (Mr. Dibb) should report that he was satisfied there was no fraud which could be brought against him. The whole thing was gross carelessness, and it was his want of caution which had brought the mountain of sus- picion against him —The Registrar said he had formed a similar opinion that serious faults had been committed, but he was inclined to think that rather more had been alleged against him than had been proved —After some observa- tions from "Sr. Davies and Mr. Rodwav the examination was again adjourned. On Thursday week application was made to his Honour Judge Ffoulkes by Arthur Edwin Hawkins, a bank- rupt, who formerly car-ied on business at 71, Bridge-street, Runcorn, as a clothier, for his discharge. From the trus- tee's report, read by the Official Receiver, it appeared that applicant was adjudicated a bankrupt in April of last year, on his own petition. The trustee reported that the total ap- parent indebtedness of the bankrupt was £1,460 odd. To- wards this £6Ol had,been realised, and the assets not yet realised were estimated to produce £2O. A first dividend of 63 in the £ had been paid, and it was expected that another of 8i in the £ would follow. The bankrupt bad omitted to keep such books of accounts as sufficiently disclosed his financial position, had contracted debts without reasonable ground for being able to pay them in full, and had brought on his bankruptcy by rash and hazardous speculation. His Honour remarked that the case was a sad one, and spoke of the serious character of the barkrupt's negligence in not keeping proper books. He should he skid, suspend the order of discharge for five years, but the bankrupt could at any time during that pe- iod renew his application, on paying to the official receiver a sum of £5O for the use of his creditors.

div.p: LA HST NE WS.

; !At the Nottingham Assizes on Friday afternoon, Robert Richardson, a middle-aged man, was sent to penal servitude for five years for coining. A whirlwind crossed the Dee at Chester, on Thursday night, strandmig many boats and demolishing a heavy gang- way from a landing stake. . . .

A Central News telegram, dated Berne. Friday, says: The village of Fiergaugen, in the canton of Valais, has been totally destroyed by tire. The report of the Merchant Shipping Commission is ex- pected next week, and it is said that there will also be a minority report in favour of the shipowners. The International cricket match, Ireland versus Canada, concluded at Dublin on Friday afternoon, with a victory for Ireland by an innings and 102 runs The drought in Cheshire and North Wales terminated on Friday morning. Rain commenced to fall all over the dis- trict early in the day, and lasted for some hours. A farmer's son named Eastson, age 14, of Wormshill, rear Sittingbourne, was sitting on a hurdle on Friday with a loaded gun in his hand when he fell, and was shot dead.

His Eminenu Henry Edward Manning, Cardinal Arch- bishop of Westminster, and a Prince of the Holy Roman Church, entered his eightieth year on Friday, having been born at Titheridge, Herts on July 15th 1803.

, ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.—The following is a list of pending elections, with dates of polling as far as fixed : Rants (Basingstoke Division), 18th met; Lambeth (Brix- ton Division), 18th met; Middlesex (Eiurnsey Division), 19th inst ; City of London, not fixed. FIRE LT CEEWE.—Lbout seven o'clock on Friday morn- ing a fire broke out in the South Cheshire Brewery, Crewe, and before it could be extinguished the whole premises were gutted, large quantities of materials ready for brewing being tlestroyed, and the boilers damaged. MURDER BY Alt Ex•SotinErt.—At Gloucester Assizes, on Friday, Baron Huddlestoa ordered the second trial of Enoch Wadley for the alleged murder of a girl named Evans near Newark, the jury having on Thursday dis- agreed, to be postponed until next assizes. in order that in- quiries may be made as to the alleged insanity of the pri- soner when a soldier in India.

;• FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—On Friday morning, another shocking colliery fatality occurred at Monk Bret- ton Colliery, near Barnsley, when Solomon Blackburn, of Belmont, Monk Bretton, was killed, and the trammer seri- ously injured. A large fall tonk place, which completely buried Blackburn, and partly overwhelmed Hurrier. So extensive was the fall, that Blackburn's body was only re- covered two hours afterwards, when it was found to be com- pletely crushed. The trammer was got out alive.

Taw aatIRDER OF A SWEETHEART AT PRESTON. At Lancaster Assizes, on Friday morning, Alfred Sow- rey, 24, pawnbroker's assistant, was charged with murder at Preston, en the 18th May, of his sweetheart, Annie Kelly. Mr. Shee, and the Hon. W. H. Cross prosecuted ; and Mr. M•Keand defended. The prisoner and Kelly had been keep- ing company for about two months and two days before the murder. Kelly left her situation as laundress at the Bull Hotel, Preston, for the purpose of being married to Sowrey land then going to America. Sowrey, on being placed in the dock, was utterly unnerved, and had to be supported on the seat by two warders. Mr. M'Keand, far the defence, set up the theory that the revolver was discharged by accident, and that the prisoner's subsequent admissions were made while in a state of horror at the fact of having unwittingly been the cause of his sweetheart's death. Mr. Justice Day then summed up at great length. The jury, after a short deliberation, returned a verdict of "guilty," and the sen- tence of death was passed in the usual form SIR GEORGE TREVELTAN AND THE LIBERAL UNIONISTS. —Sir George Trevelyan has written to the Secretary of the Bridgeton Liberal Association, Glasgow, saying that the policy of Liberals supporting Conservatives against Liberals has been carried to such an extent, that it is clearly aimed not at a settlement of the Irish question, but the suppres- sion of the Liberal party. At the January Conference it was evident that Liberals were prepared to make important concessions, but the Liberal Unionists refused to be recon- ciled to the Liberals The present Government, if well ad- vised, would have brought in a scheme free from the defects of last year's measure, based on the principle of governing Ireland something like what Irishmen asked for. Instead of this they deliberately fell to making exasperating speeches. and carried a bill for the arbitrary suppression of political speech and unity. But by keeping the Irish representa- tives he Parliament, and taking precautions for the ad- ministration of justica, we might safely establish a ttve body with the Irish execatiye for the management of Irisk affairs. •

-- WIMBLEDON RIFLE MEETING. On Friday the•competition for the St. George's Challenge Vase took place at six hundred yards. The weather was calm and the licht geod. Lieutenant Hale, 2nd Somerset, made 35, highest possible. Captain Young, 2ed Renfrew, were the Martin's Challenge Cup. A second highest possible was made for the St. George's— viz., by Corporal Fife, Ist Inverness, who followed with bull, outer, and bull with his three tie shots. Other two men—Corporal Simcack, 2nd Cheshire. and Sergeant Weir, sth Lanark—have made the highest possibles in St. George's.

div.head: NATIONAL FETE IN PARIS.
div.p: THE NATIONAL FETE IN PARIS.

PARIS, FRIDAY, 8-30 AM.—The celebration of the national fete lasted ail night, dancing being kept up at open-air balls organised in all quarters of the city until four this morning. Bower accidents are reported than in any pre- vious year, the total number of persona injured not exceed- ing three. THE BULGARIAN THRONE.

DIJERNICRTIT, FRIDAY AFT@RNOON.—Prince Ferdinand, of Coburg, replying to the Bulgarian deputation, this after- noon, said the Prince selected by Bulgaria must respect the trea'ies. He hoped they would succeed in justifying the confidence of the porte and in regaining the sympathy of Russia.

div.head: FIGHTING IN AFGHANISTAN.
div.p: FIGHTING IN AFGHANISTAN.

Accordin/, to intelligence received at Bombay through a native source, fighting has taken place between the Ameiar's troops and the rebels at Mashaki, a place south of Ghazal, a little to the east of Candahar road. The Aineer's troops were successful, taking 160 prisoners of the Ander and Tar- aki tribes, and sending 200 heads to Cabal. A large body of Jaithuri Hizrah insurgents, however, is stated to have repulsed the forces of the '<linear, who is sending reinforce- tante.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The HOUS3 met at four o'clocK.

THE COERCION BILL.—On the motion far going into Corn- mittee on the Irish Crimes Bill, Earl GRANVILLE explained his absence from the House last night, when Earl Selborne drew attention to the emptiness of the front Opposition Bench.—Earl NORTEIBROOIC challenged the leaders of the Opposition to state specifically what their alternative pelicy with regard to Ireland WaS.—Earl HOSEBERY said the opposition in their lordship's House was hopeless, and all responsibi I ity for Irlsh policy must rest on the Government. —Discussion took place on clauses 2 and C of the Crimes Bill, which passed through ComcniVee.—The third reading was fixed for Monday, and the House adjourned at half- past eight.
HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at lour o'clock.

QUESTIONS.-T he HOME SECRETARY, replying to Mr. Howell, said the Coal and Wine Dues Continuance Bill has been abandoned for the sessioa. The Government would not again intrcduce a bill, but the Metropolitan Board of Works would deal with the subject.—Mr. SAUTII intimated that if it was the general wish of the house, the Sergeant•at-Arrns would place copies of "United Ireland " in the reading. room.

div.head: CLOSURE.
div.p: CLOSURE.

The House then went in committee of supply. A vote was moved for five millions on account.—Sir JAMES • FER. GIISON, in replying to Mr. Bryce, said thee was reason to believe that there would be no ratification of the Turkish Convention, and that Sir H. Wolff would leave Constan- tinople that night. The incident, therefore, might be con- sidered closed, and the House would see it was better to postpone detailed discussion until papers were in the pos- session of hon. members, which he believed would be next day.—After a few words from IVIr. radlaugh as to adequate time being given to discuss the papers, Mr. WILLIAMSON said be was sure the country would blame the Govern- ment for having sent Sir H. Wolff to Constantinople. The discussion then turned on the vote of credit pro- posed, Mr. A. O'Colsrnort entering a strong prchest against the sys,em.—Dr. CLARE found fault with the way the Crottars' Act had been administered, especially as regarded granting loans.
Mr. T. ELLis called attention to the trial of persons

charged with complicity in disturbances at Welsh tithe evictions, and h ails condemned the manner in which the intended inquiry was to be conducted. He moved a reduc- tion of the yote.—Toe 1105 IE SECEIRTARY PAW as to the in- quiry the desire was that it should be thorough and satisfactory.—The motion to reduce the vote was with- drawn.

_ Dr. KENNY then brought the case of Mr. J. G. Fitzgerald under the notice of the committee. He said Mr Fitzgerald was formerly an inepactor of national schools in Iceland, and after a service of twenty-five veers he had been dis- missed from his poet on a charge of having misappropriated 5.3 6d. He asked for an inquiry, and moved the reduction of vote —After discussion in which Mr. Sexton, Sir J. Mc- Kenna and others took part, Mr. A. BALFOUR said there had already been an inquiry into the matter more than once, and he objected to re-open the matter.— The proposal to reduce the vote was rejected by 245 to 83. Sir J. SWINBURN was about to rase a discussioa on some other subject, wnen Mr. Small put the cloture in force, and moved that the question be new put. (Cries of 50.,, oh." from the Irish me.nners, and Ministerial cheering.) The result was—Ayes, 252; noes, 78. On the question that the vote on account be agreed to, the Committee again divided —Ayes, 242; noes, 64. The sittnag was then suspended until niee o'clock. At nine the sitting was resumed, and the House went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Esti- mates. 'I he vote for salaries and expenses of the House of Commons was agreed to after observations from Mr. Brad- ' laugh and other members on the subject of the under pay- ment of persons employed as extra messengers. The vote fur the expenses of the Treasury, including Parliamentary counsel, was prepoeed.—Mr. JACKSON, replying to Mr. A. O'Connor said it had been decided to promote a number of civil service writers to the Lower Division of establishment clerks, and, when selections had been cotnoleted, full parti- culars would be made known. No civil service writer would be forced out of the present Bernice.
