The Chairman moved the following, resolution :—" That the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners approve of the action of the Parliamentary Committee in petitioning Parliament in favour of and against alteration in a private bill, inti- tuled 'The Liverpool Waterworks and Improvement Bill e that the costa and expenses, whether already incurred or to be incurred, attendant upon such petition be charged upon the general district rate."—Mr. S. Taylor seconded the re- solution, which was unanimously passed. • On Tuesday evening, a public meeting of ratepayers was held in Bethesda Schoolroom in reference to the same sub- ject. Mr J Dobsou presided, and on the platform were Mr P Speakman, Mr W H Linaker (law clerk), and Mr E Mar- shall (secretary). Amongst the audience were Messrs J Meadowcroft, W Hankineen, H J Once, S Taylor. H White. J Pritchard, F A. Lake, J Davies, D Bisbrown, W Handley, I Handley, T Riley, Watson, J Poole, M Barker, C Dut- ton, &c. The Law Clerk at the outset explained that in 1880 the Liverpool Corporation went to Parliament to seek powers to collect large bodies of water in Montgomeryshire for the purpose of supplying Liverpool with water. After mature consideration the Runcorn Commissioners thought it right to take some steps to enable them to take a supply of water from the Liverpool Corporation mains should they require it. They decided to petition against the Bill in the House of Lords, and after several interviews with the persons act- ing on behalf of the Corporation an agreement was entered into for the benefit and protection of the town of Runcorn. The agreement read as follows :—" the Corporation agree to supply from the Vynrwy Aqueduct to the Commission- ers, as soon as any water is conveyed thereby to Liverpool, and in the event of the Commissioners having previously acquired the rigbt to supply water within the limits of the district of supply of the Runcorn Waterworks Company, or having agreed with the said company to pass any water purchased by the Commissioners from the ' Corporation through the mains of the said company, but not otherwise, any daily quantity of water, not being lees than 300,000 gallons, nor more than 1,000,000 gallons, which the Commissioners rosy from time to time require for the purpose of supplying with water the said district." They would see that in that clause Runcorn could not take water from Liverpool Corporation except the Commis- sioners either purchased the rights of the Runcorn Water- works Company, or arranged with the Waterworks Coin- pany to pass the water through their mains. Therefore the rights of the Waterworks Company were not in- fringed. The Corporation promised that next time they went to Parliament on any matter relating to Liverpool water they would insert a clause making that , agreement binding upon the Corporation, for all time. Mat- ters remained in that position until the present session,when the Corporation went to Parliament for certain extra powers with regard to the Vyrnwy water scheme, and they put in a clause confirming the agreement entered into in 1880. The bill passed through the House of Commons wittiest any movement on the part of the Runcorn Water- works Company, and it was not until the Bill had been re- printed, and passed into the House of Lords that the com- pany moved in the matter, and they then moved without notice to any body in Runcorn. The first intimation the Commissioners received of that movement was a communi- cation he received as law clerk from the town clerk of Liverpool, who stated that at the last moment the Run- corn Waterworks Company bad presented a petition against 1 the Bill. He called a meeting of the Com- missioners, and after due consideration it was con- sidered advisable that the Commisssioners should petition the House of Lords against any alteration in the Bill eo far as the agreement with the Commissioners was concerned. Such petition was prepared and presented and he and Mr. Speakman were instriected to attend in London and see that the petition was properly conducted before the Committee. He suggested to the advisers of the Company that they might take a clause whicb, while conserving any rights the Commissioners might . have under the agreement would still protect the Waterworks Company if they were not satistieA with the form in which they were protected in the Bill, in some other form. When the Bill came before the Committee an objection was taken to the locus standi of the Company on the ground that their rights were not af- fected at all, and white the argument was going on, he had the following clause handed to him by the Waterworks Company. "Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Ac contained the Corporation shalt not directly or in- directly supply water within or so as to be used within the limits for the supply of water authorised by the Runcorn, r, Weston, and Halton Waterworke Act, 1863, without the 6 consent in writing of the Runcorn, Weston, and Helton C 1 Waterworks Company, under their common seal, such con- t sent to be given upon such terms and conditions as shall be assented to by three fourths in number and value of the "4 e.l shareholders of the said Company present personally or by proxy at a meeting of the said shareholders duly convened 4. with notice of the object." SHOCKING „RAILWA t' _ACCIDENT AT WIDNE,3:

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Monday held an inquest at the Police Station, touching the death of Emily Highfleld, 6 years of age, daughter of Peter High- field, labourer, of 16, Milton-street, Widnes. Mr. R. Booth was foreman of the jury. It appeared that on Saturday afternoon, abaut half-past two, the girl was playing at the back of her father's house, along which runs a siding from the works of Messrs Elutchinson and Company and Messrs Gasket!, Deacon, and Company. A Midland Railway Com- pany's engine, having three waggons in front and eight be- hind, came along at the rate of six miles an hour, and Mrs Mary Brown, of 35. Pitt-street, saw the child entangled in the wheels of the engine She screamed, and the train was at once brought to a standstill. The body of the child was fearfully mangled, both legs and an arm having been completely severed. Death took place in a few minutes. Mrs Brown informed the jury that between the back of Milton-street and the siding there was only a few feet of space, and there was no fence erected.—Walter Rowe, brakesman, of 6, Kent-street, said he was in charge of the train, and was standing on the third wagon behind the en- gine. The enzine whistled whilst passing the houses as was customary. He did not see anyone.—Joseph Nicksou, en- gine driver, of 31, Albert-road, deposed that he did not see the deceased, but saw several other children playing about on the Pitt-street side. In reply to questions be said it was usual when wagons preceded the engine, which could not be always prevented, for a brakesrnan to be in the first wagon. It was prohibited by law to travel wagons first on the main line. His supposition was that the child ran out of an entry or back yard in Milton-street, and went between the third wagon and the engine while the train was mov- ing, otherwise there would have been marks on the wheels of the three first wagons. A vigilant look out was kept. and they would have seen the girl had she been anywhere but in an entry or back yard.—Mr. Patten, who represented the railway company, said it was customary for children to run between wagons on this siding both whilst they were standing and whilst going at a slow pace. and it was impos- s.ble to prevent accidents occurring. Although it was cus- tomary for a man to be in the firA wagon when they went before the enaine, still the brakeman in this case was fully discharging his duty, as he land gone into the third one specially to look out on the Milton-street side. At a duly convened MEETING of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, held in the TOWN HALL, WATERLOO- ROAD. RUNCORN, on TUESDAY. the TWELFTH DAY OF JULY, 1887, It was unanimously received:—" That the Run- corn Improvement Commissioners approve the action of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee in Petitioning Parlia- ment in favour of, and against, alteration in a Private Bill: entitled, The Liverpool Water works and Improvement Bill: That tt e costs and expenses, whether incurred, or to be in- curred, attendant upon tuch Petition, be charged upon the General District Rate." E. MARSHALL, Secretary. libwn Hall, Runcorn, July 14th. 1887. N PARL lAMENT, SESSION IBB7.—THE LIVERPOOL WAT:tRWORKS AND IMPROVEMENT BILL. At a MEETING of the Owners and Ratepayers of the Im- provement Act District, of RUNCORN, in the County of Chester, held on TUE,DAY, the 12th DAY OF JULY, 1887, In the BETHESDA FaIOOLROOM, VICAR STREET, RUNCORN*, such meeting being held in pursuance of an act entitled, "An Act to authorize the application of funds of Municipal Corporations and other Govern- ing Bodies in certain Cases," I, as Chairman of such Meeting, and in compliance with the statute, proposed the following resolution :—" That the Owners and Hattpayers of the Improvement Act District of Rune irn hereby approve the action of the Runcorn improvement CAnmissionero in Petitioning Parliament in favour of and against Alterations In a Private Bill intituled • The Liverpool Waterworks and Improvement BM," and that the meeting hereby sanctions the applying of the General District Rate to toe payment of the costs and expenses attending such Petition." I hereby dean.° that at such Meeting of the Owners and Ratepayers the foregoing resolution was carried. Dated at Runcorn this 14th day of July. 1887. JAMES DODSON, Summoning Officer.
